name: Fairy Parrotfish
tagline: A rainbow reef gardener with a rock-crunching beak.
intro: Fairy Parrotfish cruise the reef like colorful lawn mowers, scraping algae from hard surfaces. Their bites also grind bits of reef rock into the fine sand that washes onto beaches.
home: Warm Atlantic and Caribbean coral reefs, seagrass beds, and rocky shallows.
diet: Mostly algae and tiny organisms scraped from reef surfaces.
size: Varies by species; many are 1–3 ft (30–90 cm) long
superpower: Fused teeth form a powerful beak that scrapes rock and makes sand.
funFacts: A parrotfish beak is built from many tightly packed teeth.
New teeth replace worn ones as the fish keeps scraping.
Many parrotfish change color dramatically as they grow.
Some species sleep inside a mucus cocoon at night.
lookFor: Spot bright patchwork colors and a pale, parrot-like beak.

name: Cleaner Wrasse
tagline: The reef's tiny dentist, barber, and parasite picker.
intro: Cleaner Wrasses run busy underwater service stations where larger fish line up. They dart over each visitor, plucking parasites and loose skin from places fins cannot reach.
home: Indo-Pacific coral reefs with prominent rocks or coral heads for cleaning stations.
diet: Fish parasites, dead skin, mucus, and other tiny animal food.
size: Up to 5.5 in (14 cm) — about a pencil
superpower: It earns safe meals by cleaning animals that could easily swallow it.
funFacts: Client fish pose with open mouths or spread fins to request cleaning.
Cleaners may even enter a large fish's mouth and gill openings.
A bold dark stripe advertises the wrasse's special job.
Cleaner wrasses can use gentle fin touches to calm impatient clients.
lookFor: Find a slim fish with a dark lengthwise stripe at a busy coral station.

name: Picasso Triggerfish
tagline: A swimming artwork with a clever locking spine.
intro: Picasso Triggerfish look as if an artist painted them with bold blue, black, yellow, and white lines. They patrol shallow lagoons and can wedge themselves securely into reef cracks.
home: Shallow Indo-Pacific reef flats, sandy lagoons, and protected coral areas.
diet: Algae plus crabs, snails, worms, urchins, and other bottom animals.
size: Up to 12 in (30 cm) — about a school ruler
superpower: A second dorsal spine locks the first upright like a doorstop.
funFacts: The locking spine helps prevent predators from pulling it from a crevice.
It may sleep on its side tucked into the reef.
An alarmed fish can make a whirring sound.
Females guard patches of eggs laid on the seafloor.
lookFor: Look for diagonal face stripes and a black patch on the belly.

name: Bluestriped Grunt
tagline: A striped schooler that actually grunts underwater.
intro: Bluestriped Grunts gather in sunny yellow-and-blue schools around reefs by day. After dark they spread into seagrass and sand flats to hunt for small bottom animals.
home: Western Atlantic reefs, mangroves, and nearby seagrass beds.
diet: Crustaceans, mollusks, worms, and small fishes found at night.
size: Up to 18 in (46 cm) — about a large pillow
superpower: It grinds throat teeth to make a grunt amplified by its swim bladder.
funFacts: Its mouth lining is bright red.
Young grunts often shelter in shallow seagrass nurseries.
The blue stripes curve across a golden-yellow body.
Daytime schools may mix with other kinds of grunts.
lookFor: Find thin electric-blue stripes, yellow fins, and a red mouth.

name: White Grunt
tagline: A red-mouthed reef school makes its name by grunting.
intro: White Grunts rest in close schools over reefs and sandy bottoms during the day. After sunset, they spread into seagrass, sand, and mud to search for small animals.
home: Western Atlantic reefs and nearby seagrass beds from the Chesapeake Bay and Gulf of Mexico through the Caribbean to Brazil.
diet: Crustaceans, mollusks, echinoderms, and small fishes; juveniles also pick tiny plankton from the water.
size: Commonly about 17 in (45 cm) - a little longer than a laptop
superpower: Throat teeth grind together while the swim bladder amplifies the sound into a grunt.
funFacts: The inside of a White Grunt's mouth is bright red.
Young fish may shelter among the long spines of sea urchins.
Its colors can fade toward pale yellow to better match nearby sand or coral.
Two White Grunts may push open mouths together during a territorial display.
lookFor: Look for a silvery body, blue-striped head, forked tail, and red mouth.

name: Frogfish
tagline: A camouflaged fisher with its own wiggly lure.
intro: Frogfish can resemble sponges, algae, or lumpy rocks so closely that prey swims right past. Then the hidden hunter flicks its built-in lure and opens a giant mouth in a flash.
home: Tropical and subtropical reefs, rubble, seagrass, and sponge gardens.
diet: Fishes and crustaceans ambushed from extremely close range.
size: Most are hand-sized; the largest reach about 15 in (38 cm)
superpower: Its mouth expands suddenly, sucking prey in with rushing water.
funFacts: The lure is a modified first spine from the dorsal fin.
Some species grow skin flaps that copy nearby weeds or coral.
Frogfish often walk on stout pectoral fins instead of swimming.
Their camouflage can include both color and bumpy skin texture.
lookFor: Search for a lumpy fish with leg-like fins and a lure above its mouth.

name: Clownfish
tagline: A tiny reef neighbor protected by stinging tentacles.
intro: Clownfish live among sea anemone tentacles that sting most would-be visitors. The partnership gives the fish a fortress and can bring the anemone food, cleaning, and protection.
home: Warm Indian and Pacific Ocean reefs wherever host anemones grow.
diet: Plankton, algae, small crustaceans, and scraps from its host anemone.
size: About 2–7 in (5–18 cm), depending on species
superpower: A special mucus coating lets it safely weave through anemone stings.
funFacts: A clownfish family has one largest female and a breeding male.
If the female disappears, the breeding male can become female.
Males fan and guard eggs laid on rock near the anemone.
Clownfish make pops and clicks to communicate.
lookFor: Look for bright bands and a fish staying very close to an anemone.

name: Boxfish
tagline: A hovering fish sealed inside natural box-shaped armor.
intro: Boxfish wear a stiff shell of fused, many-sided scale plates around most of their bodies. Small fins flutter like propellers to steer the armored fish with surprising control.
home: Warm coral reefs, rocky areas, seagrass, and sandy coastal bottoms worldwide.
diet: Small invertebrates, algae, sponges, and animals uncovered in sand.
size: Usually 4–18 in (10–46 cm), depending on species
superpower: A rigid bony carapace works like a lightweight underwater suit of armor.
funFacts: Only the tail, fins, mouth, eyes, and gill areas move freely.
The armor is built from tightly joined hexagonal plates.
Some boxfish release a powerful defensive skin toxin when badly stressed.
Their small puckered mouths can blow jets of water at the sand.
lookFor: Spot a stiff boxy body, tiny fluttering fins, and puckered lips.

name: Porcupine Fish
tagline: A shy night hunter that becomes a spiky balloon.
intro: Porcupine Fish usually cruise slowly with their long spines folded against the body. When threatened, they gulp water and swell into a prickly ball that is difficult to bite.
home: Warm reefs, caves, ledges, and wrecks around the world.
diet: Nighttime meals of snails, hermit crabs, sea urchins, and other shellfish.
size: Up to 3 ft (91 cm) — about a baseball bat
superpower: Inflating makes its modified-scale spines stand straight out.
funFacts: Its fused teeth make a beak strong enough to crack shells.
The spines lie flat until the fish puffs up.
Young porcupinefish may drift in floating Sargassum seaweed.
Black spots cover both the body and fins of this species.
lookFor: Look for round eyes, a beak, black speckles, and long folding spines.

name: Lionfish
tagline: A striped ambush hunter armed with venomous spines.
intro: Lionfish drift over reefs behind a spectacular fan of striped fins. They corner small prey with those fins, then gulp it into a rapidly opening mouth.
home: Native Indo-Pacific reefs; also invasive on western Atlantic and Caribbean reefs.
diet: Small fishes, shrimp, and crabs swallowed whole.
size: Up to about 18 in (46 cm) — longer than a laptop
superpower: Venomous fin spines discourage predators while wide fins help trap prey.
funFacts: The venom is delivered by spines, not by biting.
A lionfish can spread its pectoral fins like a hunting net.
Its mouth creates suction that pulls prey inward.
Atlantic lionfish descended from aquarium releases outside their native range.
lookFor: Keep your distance from red-brown stripes and a crown of long spines.

name: Southern Flounder
tagline: A sideways sand ninja with both eyes upstairs.
intro: Southern Flounders begin life swimming upright with one eye on each side. As they grow, one eye migrates and the fish settles flat against the seafloor as a camouflaged hunter.
home: Western Atlantic bays, estuaries, rivers, and sandy coastal bottoms.
diet: Fishes, shrimp, and other crustaceans ambushed from the bottom.
size: Up to about 3 ft (90 cm) — yardstick length
superpower: It changes shade and buries itself until only its eyes show.
funFacts: Both adult eyes sit on the left side of the head.
Newly hatched larvae look more like ordinary upright fish.
Young fish use low-salinity estuaries as nursery habitat.
Sharp teeth help it seize fast-moving prey.
lookFor: Scan the sand for two raised eyes and the outline of a flat body.

name: Sargeant Major
tagline: A striped reef guard with military-looking bars.
intro: Sargeant Majors zip around reefs in silvery schools, flashing yellow backs and five dark bars. Their name comes from those bars, which resemble the rank marks of a military sergeant major.
home: Western Atlantic reefs, rocks, wrecks, pilings, and floating Sargassum.
diet: Algae, plankton, small crustaceans, larvae, and fish eggs.
size: Up to 9 in (23 cm) — about a dinner plate across
superpower: A guarding male fearlessly chases intruders away from his egg patch.
funFacts: The accepted common spelling is Sergeant Major.
Males darken to bluish colors while guarding eggs.
Females attach purple eggs to cleaned rock surfaces.
Young fish may shelter beneath drifting mats of Sargassum.
lookFor: Count five bold black bars across a yellow-topped silver body.

name: French Angelfish
tagline: A golden-edged sponge snacker that often swims in pairs.
intro: French Angelfish glide over Caribbean reefs in close pairs, showing yellow-rimmed scales against a dark body. Youngsters look completely different and may work as cleaners for much larger fish.
home: Shallow western Atlantic and Caribbean coral and rocky reefs.
diet: Mostly sponges, plus algae, tunicates, coral animals, and other invertebrates.
size: Up to 24 in (61 cm) — about a carry-on suitcase
superpower: Comb-like teeth nip tiny pieces from tough, springy sponges.
funFacts: Adults commonly travel in long-lasting pairs.
Each dark adult scale has a bright golden-yellow edge.
Juveniles are black with curved yellow bands.
Young French Angelfish pick parasites from visiting reef fish.
lookFor: Find a dark disk-shaped fish with glowing yellow scale edges.

name: Spanish Hogfish
tagline: A purple-and-yellow wrasse with a rooting piglike snout.
intro: Spanish Hogfish sweep their pointed snouts over the reef while searching for crunchy prey. Younger fish also visit cleaning stations, where they pick parasites from larger neighbors.
home: Western Atlantic and Caribbean coral reefs, rocky ledges, and drop-offs.
diet: Crabs, snails, brittle stars, urchins, worms, and other hard-bottom animals.
size: Up to about 16 in (40 cm) — forearm length
superpower: Strong jaws and a probing snout uncover and crush hidden invertebrates.
funFacts: Spanish Hogfish belong to the wrasse family.
Adults are yellow behind and purple-red toward the head.
Juveniles can advertise cleaning by moving conspicuously above the reef.
Like many wrasses, an individual can change from female to male.
lookFor: Look for a sharp color split: purple-red front and yellow rear.

name: Twinspot Butterflyfish
tagline: A fluttering reef disk decorated with two clever false eyes.
intro: Twinspot Butterflyfish slip between coral branches with thin bodies that turn edge-on in a blink. Dark spots near the tail can confuse a predator about which end will dart away first.
home: Warm coral reefs and lagoons, including the Red Sea and Indo-Pacific.
diet: Coral polyps, tiny invertebrates, plankton, algae, or fish eggs, depending on species.
size: Around 5 in (13 cm) — about a child's hand
superpower: A paper-thin body pivots through coral while eyespots misdirect attackers.
funFacts: Butterflyfish have small mouths filled with brushlike teeth.
Many species wear a dark stripe across the real eye.
Most feed during daylight and shelter after dark.
Many adult butterflyfish travel in bonded pairs.
lookFor: Spot a thin round body, an eye stripe, and two dark tailward spots.

name: Queen Angelfish
tagline: A royal-blue reef beauty wearing a tiny forehead crown.
intro: Queen Angelfish glow blue and yellow as they weave around Caribbean reefs. A ringed spot on the forehead resembles a crown, perfectly matching this fish's royal name.
home: Warm western Atlantic coral reefs from Florida and Bermuda to Brazil.
diet: Mostly sponges, with tunicates, algae, jellylike animals, and other reef life.
size: Up to 18 in (46 cm) — about a laptop
superpower: Its narrow body and brushlike teeth reach sponge food in reef cracks.
funFacts: The crown is a blue-ringed dark spot above the eyes.
Young Queen Angelfish clean parasites from larger fishes.
Juveniles are dark blue with bright curved bars.
Queen and Blue Angelfish can produce natural hybrids.
lookFor: Find a yellow tail, electric-blue edges, and a forehead crown.

name: Blue Tang
tagline: A blue reef grazer carrying a hidden tail scalpel.
intro: Atlantic Blue Tangs roam Caribbean reefs, clipping algae from rock and coral in busy groups. A sharp spine beside the tail swings outward for defense like a tiny surgeon's blade.
home: Western Atlantic coral reefs and rocky shores, especially in the Caribbean.
diet: Mostly algae scraped or nipped from hard reef surfaces.
size: Up to about 15 in (38 cm) — longer than a ruler
superpower: A razor-edged tail spine flashes out when danger gets too close.
funFacts: Young Atlantic Blue Tangs are bright yellow, not blue.
Growing juveniles pass through a mixed yellow-and-blue stage.
Groups sometimes follow grazing parrotfish to reach newly exposed algae.
Its flattened body slips easily through narrow reef passages.
lookFor: Look for an oval blue body and a pale blade beside the tail.

name: Spectacled Parrotfish
tagline: A Hawaiian reef grazer wearing colorful eye spectacles.
intro: Spectacled Parrotfish scrape algae from clear Hawaiian reefs with a sturdy dental beak. Large adults develop dramatic markings around the eyes that look like a pair of painted goggles.
home: Clear lagoons and outer reefs around Hawaiʻi and nearby central Pacific islands.
diet: Algae and other growth scraped from coral rock.
size: Up to about 2 ft (61 cm) — roughly pillow length
superpower: Its beak clears algae and opens bare reef space for new growth.
funFacts: This species is native to the Hawaiian region and nearby islands.
It can live from shallow reef flats down to deeper reef slopes.
Spectacled Parrotfish begin adult life as females and some become males.
Breeding pairs release eggs that drift in open water.
lookFor: Look for a parrot beak and bold mask-like markings around the eyes.

name: Green Moray Eel
tagline: A crevice hunter with a second set of jaws.
intro: Green Moray Eels wind through reef cracks and wait with only their heads showing. When prey comes close, a hidden second pair of jaws shoots forward from the throat to pull the meal in.
home: Western Atlantic reefs, rocky shores, mangroves, and seagrass beds.
diet: Fishes, crabs, shrimp, octopuses, and other reef animals.
size: Up to about 8 ft (2.4 m) — taller than a doorway
superpower: Mobile throat jaws grab prey and carry it into the eel's mouth.
funFacts: Its skin is naturally gray-brown, but yellow mucus makes it look green.
An open mouth usually means the eel is pumping water over its gills.
Morays have smooth, scaleless skin protected by slippery mucus.
They spend much of the day hidden and often hunt after dark.
lookFor: Watch reef holes for a large green head with a constantly opening mouth.

name: Reef Shark
tagline: A shallow-water shark with ink-dipped fin tips.
intro: Reef Sharks patrol warm lagoons and reef edges, often in water barely deeper than their bodies. Their bold black fin tips make them one of the easiest sharks to recognize.
home: Shallow Indo-Pacific coral reefs, lagoons, and sandy reef flats.
diet: Mostly reef fishes, plus squid, octopuses, shrimp, and crabs.
size: Up to about 6 ft (1.8 m) — adult-human length
superpower: Quick turns and bursts of speed make it a brilliant shallow-reef hunter.
funFacts: The first dorsal fin has a black tip with a pale band beneath it.
Young sharks use very shallow lagoons as nurseries.
Females give birth to live pups rather than laying eggs.
Many individuals repeatedly patrol the same small home area.
lookFor: Check the dorsal and tail fins for sharply painted black tips.

name: Great Barracuda
tagline: A silver torpedo built for lightning-fast ambushes.
intro: Great Barracudas hover almost motionless near reefs before exploding forward after a fish. Their long jaws carry fanglike teeth that fit into gaps in the opposite jaw.
home: Tropical Atlantic reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, and coastal open water.
diet: Fishes, especially schooling species, plus occasional squid and crustaceans.
size: Up to about 6.5 ft (2 m) — longer than a bed
superpower: A streamlined body launches from stillness into a sudden high-speed strike.
funFacts: Adults often hunt alone, while younger barracudas may gather in groups.
Juveniles shelter in mangroves and seagrass before moving toward reefs.
Dark body spots become more obvious on large adults.
Its lower jaw sticks out beyond the upper jaw.
lookFor: Spot a long silver body, pointed head, dark spots, and underslung jaw.

name: Goliath Grouper
tagline: A reef giant with a vacuum-powered gulp.
intro: Goliath Groupers are enormous, thick-bodied fish that rest around reefs, wrecks, and ledges. A sudden opening of the mouth creates suction strong enough to sweep prey inside.
home: Western Atlantic reefs and wrecks; juveniles grow in mangrove nurseries.
diet: Crabs, lobsters, fishes, octopuses, and other large reef prey.
size: Up to about 8 ft (2.4 m) and 800 lb (363 kg)
superpower: It expands its mouth and throat into a powerful underwater vacuum.
funFacts: Goliath Groupers can make booming sounds with their swim bladders.
Young fish spend several years among tangled mangrove roots.
Adults gather at special offshore sites to spawn.
Despite the teeth, suction does most of the work when catching prey.
lookFor: Look for a huge rounded fish with small dark spots and broad fins.

name: Green Sea Turtle
tagline: A long-distance reef traveler powered by seagrass.
intro: Green Sea Turtles glide over reefs with winglike front flippers and surface to breathe air. Adults are unusual among sea turtles because they eat mostly plants.
home: Tropical and subtropical coasts, reefs, lagoons, and seagrass meadows worldwide.
diet: Adults mainly eat seagrass and algae; youngsters eat a wider mix.
size: Shell up to about 4 ft (1.2 m); often 250–350 lb
superpower: It navigates across entire ocean regions between feeding and nesting grounds.
funFacts: The name refers to greenish body fat, not shell color.
Sea turtles cannot pull their heads and flippers inside their shells.
Females usually return near their birth beaches to lay eggs.
Healthy seagrass stays productive when turtles crop it like a lawn.
lookFor: Notice a smooth oval shell and a small rounded head with one scale pair between the eyes.

name: Spinner Dolphins
tagline: Acrobatic night hunters that spin above the waves.
intro: Spinner Dolphins hunt small deep-water animals at night, then rest together in sheltered daytime bays. Their famous leaps can include several complete corkscrew turns before splashdown.
home: Tropical oceans worldwide, with some groups resting near islands and reefs.
diet: Small fishes, squid, and shrimp that rise toward the surface at night.
size: About 4–7 ft (1.2–2.1 m) — bicycle to sofa length
superpower: A powerful leap becomes a rapid midair spin used in social signaling.
funFacts: One leap may include as many as four full body revolutions.
Their long scientific species name means long-snouted.
They use whistles and clicks to stay in contact and find prey.
Many have a three-part pattern: dark back, gray sides, and pale belly.
lookFor: Watch for a slender beak, three-tone body, and corkscrew leaps.

name: Manta Ray
tagline: A flying carpet that filters tiny ocean snacks.
intro: Manta Rays soar over reefs on enormous triangular fins, banking like birds underwater. Horn-shaped head fins unroll to funnel plankton-rich water into a wide, harmless mouth.
home: Tropical Indo-Pacific reefs, lagoons, channels, and nearby open water.
diet: Mostly zooplankton, including tiny drifting crustaceans and larvae.
size: Wingspan up to about 18 ft (5.5 m) — wider than a car
superpower: Cephalic fins steer clouds of plankton toward its filtering gill plates.
funFacts: Each manta's belly has a unique spot pattern, like a fingerprint.
Mantas repeatedly visit reef cleaning stations to have parasites removed.
They are rays, but they do not have a stinging tail spine.
Mantas sometimes leap completely out of the water.
lookFor: Look for broad black wings, two head fins, and belly spots.

name: Sea Urchin
tagline: A spiky reef gardener with five self-sharpening teeth.
intro: Long-spined Sea Urchins emerge after dark to graze algae from Caribbean reefs. Their extra-long movable spines protect the urchin and can shelter tiny fishes between them.
home: Western Atlantic and Caribbean coral and rocky reefs, ledges, and crevices.
diet: Mostly reef algae, with occasional tiny animals or drifting food.
size: Body up to 4 in (10 cm); spines can reach 12 in (30 cm)
superpower: Five hard teeth scrape algae and help keep space open for corals.
funFacts: The hard round inner shell is called a test.
Its jaw apparatus is nicknamed Aristotle's lantern.
Hundreds of tube feet work like tiny hydraulic suction cups.
It senses passing shadows and points its spines toward possible danger.
lookFor: Look into reef cracks for a black center surrounded by needle-long spines.

name: Anemone
tagline: A stinging sea animal disguised as a flower.
intro: Sea Anemones may look like swaying flowers, but they are animal cousins of corals and jellyfish. Their tentacles fire microscopic stinging capsules that capture prey and discourage hungry visitors.
home: Seafloors worldwide, from sunlit reefs and tide pools to the deep ocean.
diet: Plankton, shrimp, small fishes, and other animals caught by tentacles.
size: From under 0.5 in to several feet across, depending on species
superpower: Thousands of tiny nematocysts fire harpoonlike threads on contact.
funFacts: Anemones have one body opening for both food and waste.
A sticky foot anchors the body, but many can slowly glide to a new spot.
Some host clownfish, shrimp, algae, or other helpful partners.
They have no brain; a spread-out nerve net coordinates their movements.
lookFor: Find a soft column topped by a circle of waving tentacles.

name: Emerald Crab
tagline: A tiny green reef custodian with spoon-shaped claws.
intro: Emerald Crabs blend into Caribbean algae with a deep green shell and fuzzy legs. They spend much of the night picking edible growth and scraps from rock and coral crevices.
home: Caribbean and western Atlantic reefs, rubble, rocks, and seagrass.
diet: Algae, detritus, leftover food, and tiny invertebrates.
size: Shell about 1.5 in (4 cm) across — cookie-sized
superpower: Flattened claw tips scrape algae from rough places other grazers miss.
funFacts: Its green color provides camouflage among algae.
Bristly legs help collect food and break up the crab's outline.
Like other crabs, it must molt its hard shell to grow.
A female carries developing eggs beneath her folded abdomen.
lookFor: Peer under reef ledges for green claws and hairy walking legs.

name: Blue Crab
tagline: A sideways swimmer with blue claws and paddle feet.
intro: Blue Crabs scuttle and swim through bays using their flattened rear legs like paddles. They are quick, curious omnivores that investigate almost anything edible on the bottom.
home: Western Atlantic estuaries, seagrass beds, marshes, bays, and coastal shallows.
diet: Clams, oysters, worms, small animals, carrion, plants, and detritus.
size: Shell up to about 9 in (23 cm) across — dinner-plate width
superpower: Paddle-shaped back legs turn a bottom-walking crab into a strong swimmer.
funFacts: Its scientific name means beautiful savory swimmer.
Adult males have blue claws; mature females often have red-orange tips.
A soft-shell crab is simply a blue crab soon after molting.
Females move toward saltier water before releasing their larvae.
lookFor: Spot olive shell, blue claws, side spikes, and rear swimming paddles.

name: Arrow Crab
tagline: A tiny reef spider with an arrow-shaped nose.
intro: Arrow Crabs tiptoe over Caribbean reefs on extremely long, skinny legs. Their triangular bodies and pointed rostrums make them look like animated arrows or underwater spiders.
home: Atlantic and Caribbean reefs, hiding in sponges, corals, anemones, and crevices.
diet: Small worms and invertebrates, algae, detritus, and scavenged scraps.
size: Body 1–2.5 in (2.5–6 cm); legs reach about 4 in (10 cm)
superpower: Stiltlike legs let it pick through tight reef hiding places at night.
funFacts: Arrow Crabs are true crabs, not spiders.
They usually hide by day and forage after dark.
The long pointed snout is called a rostrum.
Their delicate-looking walking legs can be more than three times body length.
lookFor: Search for a tiny striped triangle balanced on eight spidery legs.

name: Mantis Shrimp
tagline: A rainbow-eyed crustacean with spring-loaded hunting arms.
intro: Mantis Shrimp are not true shrimp but a separate group of fierce, burrow-dwelling crustaceans. Some smash shells with clubs, while others spear prey with barbed folding arms.
home: Mostly warm shallow seas, living in coral, rock, sand, or mud burrows.
diet: Snails, crabs, clams, shrimp, worms, and fishes.
size: About 1–12 in (3–30 cm), depending on species
superpower: Some spring-loaded clubs strike so fast they create collapsing bubbles.
funFacts: Smasher species use clubs, while spearers use sharp spines.
Each stalked eye can move independently.
A single eye can judge distance without help from the other.
Many species detect ultraviolet and polarized light that people cannot see.
lookFor: Look for movable stalked eyes and folded mantis-like hunting arms.

name: Leather Starfish
tagline: A soft sea star that smells surprisingly garlicky.
intro: Leather Starfish feel smooth and slippery because mucus coats their unusually soft upper surface. They creep across cool Pacific seafloors hunting anemones and other invertebrates.
home: Rocky and sandy shallows from Alaska to northern Mexico.
diet: Sea anemones, urchins, sponges, sea cucumbers, and other invertebrates.
size: Up to 10 in (25 cm) across — dinner-plate width
superpower: It turns its stomach outward to digest prey outside its body.
funFacts: Its wet-leather texture gives the species its name.
Out of water, it may smell like garlic or spent fireworks.
A small scale worm sometimes rides beneath the star.
Some swimming anemones detach and flee when a Leather Star touches them.
lookFor: Find five broad arms with smooth mottled red, brown, and gray skin.

name: Cleaner Shrimp
tagline: A see-through reef hygienist waving extra-long antennae.
intro: Cleaner Shrimp advertise their services by rocking and sweeping long white antennae. Visiting fish pause while the shrimp picks parasites and damaged tissue from skin, gills, and even mouths.
home: Caribbean and western Atlantic reefs, usually beside a host sea anemone.
diet: Fish parasites, damaged tissue, mucus, plankton, and tiny food scraps.
size: Body about 1 in (2.5 cm), with much longer antennae
superpower: Its cleaning dance convinces hungry fish to become peaceful customers.
funFacts: The nearly transparent body carries blue-violet markings.
Long white antennae act like a cleaning-station sign.
It slowly acclimates to its host anemone's stinging tentacles.
Client fish may hold still and open their mouths for service.
lookFor: Search anemones for a glass-clear shrimp waving two long white antennae.

name: Crown of Thorns
tagline: A many-armed coral eater covered in venomous thorns.
intro: Crown of Thorns sea stars are native coral predators on Indo-Pacific reefs. Normal numbers are part of nature, but huge outbreaks can eat living coral faster than a reef can replace it.
home: Indo-Pacific coral reefs, including Australia's Great Barrier Reef.
diet: Living tissue from hard corals, especially branching and table corals.
size: Commonly 10–14 in; exceptional adults approach 3 ft (1 m) across
superpower: It spreads its stomach over a coral colony and digests tissue outside its body.
funFacts: Adults usually have far more than the five arms of a familiar sea star.
A light-sensitive eyespot sits at the end of every arm.
Water-powered tube feet carry it across the reef.
Giant triton snails and several reef fishes can eat this spiny star.
lookFor: Recognize a broad disk packed with many arms and long needlelike spines.

name: Nudibranch
tagline: A shell-free sea slug dressed in impossible colors.
intro: Nudibranchs are soft sea slugs whose dazzling colors can advertise danger or hide them in plain sight. Each species has a favorite menu, from sponges and hydroids to anemones and even other nudibranchs.
home: Oceans worldwide, from tide pools and coral reefs to the deep seafloor.
diet: Sponges, hydroids, anemones, bryozoans, eggs, or other slugs, by species.
size: From rice-grain tiny to about 12 in (30 cm); many are thumb-sized
superpower: Some steal unfired stinging cells from prey and reuse them for defense.
funFacts: Adult nudibranchs have no protective outer shell.
The name means naked gills, referring to exposed breathing structures.
Head horns called rhinophores sense chemicals dissolved in water.
Every nudibranch has both male and female reproductive organs.
lookFor: Look for a colorful slug with bunny-ear rhinophores or feathery back gills.

name: Giant Triton
tagline: A giant hunting snail that tackles thorny sea stars.
intro: Giant Tritons are huge reef snails that track sea stars across Indo-Pacific reefs. A muscular foot grips the prey while a ribbon of tiny teeth rasps through its defenses.
home: Tropical Indo-Pacific reefs, including the Red Sea and Pacific islands.
diet: Sea stars, including crown-of-thorns, plus other echinoderms.
size: Shell up to about 18–20 in (46–50 cm) — backpack length
superpower: It tolerates crown-of-thorns defenses and eats this formidable coral predator.
funFacts: The tooth-covered feeding ribbon is called a radula.
Its beautiful spiral shell is one of the largest made by a living snail.
People in several Pacific cultures have used empty shells as trumpets.
A crown-of-thorns sea star may flee when it detects a triton's scent.
lookFor: Spot a huge pointed spiral shell patterned cream, brown, and orange.

name: Octopus
tagline: A soft-bodied puzzle solver with eight sensing arms.
intro: Octopuses explore reefs with curious arms lined by powerful, taste-sensitive suckers. Their skin can change color, pattern, and bumpiness in moments to hide or communicate.
home: Every ocean, in dens among reefs, rocks, shells, sand, and deep seafloors.
diet: Crabs, clams, snails, shrimp, fishes, and other animals.
size: Species range from fingertip-sized to arm spans over 20 ft (6 m)
superpower: Color cells and shape-shifting skin create camouflage in a blink.
funFacts: An octopus has three hearts.
Copper-rich blood carries oxygen and makes the blood look blue.
The beak is the main hard body part, so the rest can squeeze through tight gaps.
Many octopuses jet away by blasting water through a funnel.
lookFor: Watch for eight sucker-lined arms and eyes peeking from a shell-strewn den.

name: Oysters
tagline: Living water filters that build bustling shell cities.
intro: Oysters draw water across their gills, trapping tiny food while helping clear the water. Generations attach to older shells and build rough reefs filled with hiding places for fish and crabs.
home: Shallow salty and brackish coasts, bays, estuaries, and tidal creeks worldwide.
diet: Microscopic algae and organic particles filtered from the water.
size: Often 3–10 in (8–25 cm), depending on species and age
superpower: Under good conditions, one adult can filter up to 50 gallons daily.
funFacts: Oysters are bivalves, meaning two shells hinge together.
Free-swimming larvae become spat after cementing to a hard surface.
Young oysters often settle directly on older oyster shells.
Reef crevices shelter small fishes, shrimp, crabs, and other animals.
lookFor: Find clusters of rough, uneven shells cemented together in shallow water.

name: Giant Clam
tagline: The world's biggest bivalve, powered partly by sunshine.
intro: Giant Clams sit in bright reef shallows with a colorful mantle spread toward the sun. Tiny algae living safely in their tissues make sugars that help these mollusks grow enormous.
home: Shallow Indo-Pacific coral reefs, lagoons, sand, and hard reef flats.
diet: Food made by partner algae plus plankton filtered from water.
size: Up to 4.25 ft (1.3 m) and about 550 lb (250 kg)
superpower: A partnership with sun-powered algae supplies much of its food.
funFacts: It is the largest living bivalve on Earth.
A settled adult stays in the same patch of reef for life.
Tiny light-sensitive eyes dot the edge of the colorful mantle.
No verified human death has ever been caused by a Giant Clam.
lookFor: Look for a deeply folded shell and a blue-green patterned mantle.

name: Great White
tagline: A warm-muscled ocean hunter with rows of replacement teeth.
intro: Great Whites are powerful, wide-ranging sharks that patrol coasts and offshore waters around the world. Dark backs hide them from above while pale bellies blend with the bright surface from below.
home: Cool-temperate and subtropical coastal and offshore waters worldwide.
diet: Fishes, rays, other sharks, seals, sea lions, and carrion.
size: Up to about 20 ft (6 m) — longer than a family car
superpower: Heat-producing muscles keep key body parts warmer than the surrounding sea.
funFacts: A Great White's skeleton is cartilage, not bone.
Rows of new teeth rotate forward when old teeth are lost.
Some launch completely out of the water while chasing fast prey.
They can travel thousands of miles across open ocean.
lookFor: Notice a cone-shaped snout and a sharp gray-to-white color boundary.

name: Tiger Shark
tagline: A striped night hunter with can-opener teeth.
intro: Tiger Sharks cruise warm coasts with broad heads and dark bars along their backs. Their unusually varied menu makes them important scavengers as well as formidable hunters.
home: Tropical and warm-temperate coasts, reefs, lagoons, and open water worldwide.
diet: Fishes, rays, turtles, seabirds, marine mammals, crustaceans, and carrion.
size: Commonly 10–14 ft; very large sharks exceed 18 ft (5.5 m)
superpower: Deeply notched, serrated teeth can slice through shell, hide, and bone.
funFacts: Young Tiger Sharks have spots and bars that resemble a tiger's pattern.
The markings usually fade as the shark ages.
A broad blunt snout holds sensory pores that detect hidden prey.
Tiger Sharks often become more active after sunset.
lookFor: Look for a blunt head and shadowy vertical bars on the sides.

name: Hammerhead
tagline: A living metal detector with eyes spread wide.
intro: Hammerhead Sharks carry a flattened head called a cephalofoil, with an eye near each end. That remarkable shape spreads sensory organs across a wide search area and helps the shark maneuver.
home: Warm coastal and offshore seas, including reefs, bays, and continental shelves.
diet: Fishes, squid, crustaceans, other sharks, and especially rays for some species.
size: Roughly 3–20 ft (0.9–6 m), depending on species
superpower: A wide sensor-packed head detects tiny electrical fields from buried prey.
funFacts: There are several species of hammerhead, from bonnetheads to great hammerheads.
Widely spaced eyes give hammerheads an exceptionally broad view.
Some species form large daytime schools, then hunt separately at night.
A hammerhead may pin a ray against the bottom with its head.
lookFor: The unmistakable clue is a flattened hammer-shaped head with wide-set eyes.

name: Bull Shark
tagline: A stocky sea shark equally comfortable upriver.
intro: Bull Sharks are muscular coastal sharks with blunt snouts and a remarkable tolerance for fresh water. They enter bays, estuaries, and rivers, sometimes traveling far inland.
home: Warm coastal seas, estuaries, river mouths, and some freshwater rivers and lakes.
diet: Fishes, rays, turtles, dolphins, crustaceans, birds, and other sharks.
size: Up to about 11.5 ft (3.5 m) — longer than two bicycles
superpower: Special kidneys and glands balance salt and water as salinity changes.
funFacts: Few sharks move between salt water and fresh water so readily.
Young Bull Sharks use shallow estuaries and lagoons as nurseries.
Their small eyes suit the murky water where they often hunt.
Females give birth to live pups connected by placentas before birth.
lookFor: Look for a stout gray body, very blunt snout, and small eyes.

name: Bottlenose Dolphin
tagline: A social echo-hunter with a signature whistle.
intro: Bottlenose Dolphins are clever marine mammals that breathe air and raise their calves with milk. Pods cooperate, communicate, and use echoes to map prey even when the water is dark or cloudy.
home: Temperate and tropical coasts, bays, estuaries, reefs, and offshore waters worldwide.
diet: Fishes, squid, and crustaceans caught alone or by cooperative hunting.
size: Usually 6–13 ft (1.8–4 m), depending on population
superpower: Echolocation turns returning clicks into a detailed sound-picture of nearby objects.
funFacts: Each dolphin develops a distinctive signature whistle that can act like a name.
A single blowhole on top of the head leads to the lungs.
Dolphins can rest one half of the brain while the other stays alert.
Some pods herd fish into tight groups before taking turns feeding.
lookFor: Watch for a curved dorsal fin, gray body, and short bottle-shaped beak.

name: Bristlemouth
tagline: Tiny lights, tiny teeth, enormous numbers.
intro: A bristlemouth is a finger-sized fish with a surprisingly toothy grin. Huge swarms of these little glow-fish cruise through the dark ocean every day.
home: It lives in deep midwater around the world, often hundreds of meters down.
diet: It eats tiny crustaceans and other drifting animals.
size: Usually under 3 in (8 cm)—shorter than a crayon
superpower: Rows of photophores help it signal and hide in the darkness.
funFacts: Scientists think Cyclothone may be the most abundant vertebrate genus on Earth.
Its fine teeth look like the bristles of a brush.
Neat rows of light organs run along its belly and sides.
Even its eggs and larvae drift as part of the plankton.
lookFor: Look for a slim dark body, bristly teeth, and dotted rows of lights.

name: Owlfish
tagline: Dinner-plate eyes scan the midnight water.
intro: Owlfish seem to be wearing enormous night-vision goggles. Their oversized eyes gather the faint scraps of light that reach the deep sea.
home: They roam deep midwater in oceans worldwide, from about 550 to 6,600 meters down.
diet: They snap up shrimp, small jellies, and other tiny drifting animals.
size: Around 6 in (15 cm)—about pencil-length
superpower: Extra-large eyes spot silhouettes and flashes that smaller eyes might miss.
funFacts: Owlfish belong to the deep-sea smelt family, Bathylagidae.
Their eyes take up much of the head and aim mostly upward.
Some members of the family have been found more than 6 kilometers deep.
A lightweight, soft body helps save energy where meals are scarce.
lookFor: The enormous round eyes and small silvery-brown body are the best clues.

name: Pacific Grenadier
tagline: A patient scavenger with a ribbon-like tail.
intro: The Pacific grenadier patrols the seafloor like a deep-sea cleanup crew. Its big head narrows into a long tail instead of ending in a normal tail fin.
home: It lives along North Pacific continental slopes about 300 to 3,700 meters deep.
diet: It eats fishes, squid, crustaceans, worms, and carrion.
size: Usually 18–26 in (46–65 cm)—about baseball-bat length
superpower: A keen sense of smell helps it locate scattered meals in black water.
funFacts: Grenadiers are relatives of cod.
The skinny pointed tail earns them the nickname rattails.
Pacific grenadiers can live for more than 70 years.
They are among the most common large fishes on parts of the Pacific slope.
lookFor: Spot the bulky head, large eyes, and tail that tapers to a thread.

name: Viperfish
tagline: Needle fangs turn darkness into a trap.
intro: The viperfish looks like a pocket-sized sea monster, but it is only about ruler-length. It waits almost motionless, then darts at prey with a lightning-fast strike.
home: It ranges through tropical and temperate deep waters worldwide, often 500 to 2,500 meters down by day.
diet: It hunts small fishes and crustaceans.
size: Up to about 12 in (30 cm)—one classroom ruler
superpower: A huge hinged mouth and cage-like fangs clamp around slippery prey.
funFacts: Its longest teeth are so big that they curve outside the closed mouth.
A glowing tip on its first dorsal-fin ray may help tempt prey closer.
Rows of belly lights camouflage it against the faint glow above.
Many viperfish rise toward shallower water at night and sink again by day.
lookFor: Look for long needle teeth, a large lower jaw, and dotted belly lights.

name: Barrel Eye Fish
tagline: A clear head hides swiveling green eyes.
intro: The barreleye peers through a transparent, fluid-filled shield over its head. Its glowing green tube-shaped eyes can point upward for searching or forward for eating.
home: It hovers in North Pacific midwater, usually about 600 to 800 meters deep.
diet: It eats tiny crustaceans and animals caught among jelly-like siphonophores.
size: About 6 in (15 cm)—roughly pencil-length
superpower: Rotating tubular eyes scan above and then swing forward for a meal.
funFacts: The two dark dots above its mouth are smell organs, not eyes.
Green pigment in the eyes filters the faint light from above.
Broad flat fins let it hover almost perfectly still.
Scientists first filmed its living transparent head in the wild in 2004.
lookFor: Find the clear head dome with two bright green cylinders inside.

name: Fangtooth Fish
tagline: The ocean's biggest grin fits in your hand.
intro: The fangtooth packs an enormous set of teeth into a fish no longer than a banana. It cruises dark water with a tough body built for pressure and chilly temperatures.
home: It lives in tropical and temperate oceans worldwide, from about 500 to nearly 5,000 meters deep.
diet: Adults eat fishes and squid, while youngsters begin with tiny crustaceans.
size: Up to about 6 in (16 cm)—banana-sized
superpower: Oversized teeth lock into special head pockets so the mouth can close.
funFacts: Its teeth are among the largest of any fish compared with body size.
Pockets in the roof of its mouth keep the lower fangs from piercing its brain.
Young fangtooths look so different that scientists once gave them another name.
Unlike many neighbors, it has no glowing photophores.
lookFor: The huge lower fangs, blocky head, and small dark body are unmistakable.

name: Black Swallower
tagline: A stretchy belly makes every meal supersized.
intro: The black swallower has a small body and a wildly expandable stomach. It can gulp down a fish larger than itself, then slowly digest the enormous meal.
home: It swims in deep tropical and subtropical waters around the world.
diet: It eats other bony fishes, including prey larger than its own body.
size: Up to about 10 in (25 cm)—about dinner-plate length
superpower: Hinged jaws and a balloon-like stomach let it swallow gigantic prey.
funFacts: Backward-pointing teeth keep a captured fish from wriggling out.
Its stomach wall becomes almost transparent when stretched around a meal.
If oversized prey spoils before digestion, gas can float the swallower to the surface.
The dark body hides it in the midnight zone between meals.
lookFor: Look for a slender black fish with a huge sagging belly after feeding.

name: Tripod Fish
tagline: Living stilts turn the seafloor into a lookout.
intro: The tripod fish balances above the mud on three incredibly long fin rays. Facing the current, it waits for food to drift into reach of its feeler-like fins.
home: It stands on soft deep seafloors worldwide, usually 900 to 4,700 meters down.
diet: It catches tiny crustaceans and small fishes carried past by the current.
size: Body about 12 in (30 cm); stilts can approach 3 ft (1 m)
superpower: It pumps fluid into flexible fin rays to stiffen them into stilts.
funFacts: Two pelvic-fin rays and one tail ray form the three-legged stand.
Tiny eyes are less useful than touch in its pitch-black home.
Long pectoral fins sense movement and guide food toward the mouth.
Young tripod fish drift near the surface before moving into the deep.
lookFor: Find the fish perched above mud on three wire-thin legs.

name: Coelacanth
tagline: An ancient fish rediscovered in modern seas.
intro: For millions of years, people knew coelacanths only from fossils and thought they had vanished. Then a living one astonished scientists in 1938.
home: The African coelacanth shelters in deep caves along rocky western Indian Ocean slopes.
diet: It drifts after fishes, squid, and other cephalopods at night.
size: Up to about 6.5 ft (2 m)—taller than most adults
superpower: Fleshy paired fins swing in an alternating pattern like four underwater limbs.
funFacts: Only two living coelacanth species are known today.
Its lineage appears in fossils more than 360 million years old.
A special joint inside the skull helps open its mouth wide.
Females produce live young after the eggs develop inside their bodies.
lookFor: Notice the thick lobed fins, white speckles, and three-lobed tail.

name: Anglerfish
tagline: A glowing fishing rod hangs over a hungry mouth.
intro: The female humpback anglerfish carries her own fishing pole on her forehead. A glowing lure draws curious prey close enough for one sudden gulp.
home: It roams deep tropical and temperate oceans worldwide, from about 100 to 4,500 meters down.
diet: It ambushes fishes and crustaceans that approach its lure.
size: Females up to about 8 in (20 cm)—about hand-length
superpower: Its bioluminescent lure turns total darkness into a hunting advantage.
funFacts: The glowing lure is a modified spine called an illicium.
Females can stretch their jaws and stomachs around surprisingly large meals.
Males are tiny compared with females and use an excellent sense of smell to find them.
MBARI recorded the first video of this species in its deep habitat in 2014.
lookFor: Look for a round black body, needle teeth, and one bright forehead lure.

name: Chimera
tagline: A ghostly shark cousin with crushing tooth plates.
intro: Chimeras are ancient relatives of sharks and rays with silvery, otherworldly bodies. Instead of rows of replaceable shark teeth, they carry sturdy plates for crushing food.
home: Most species cruise cold continental slopes and deep seafloors around the world.
diet: They crush crabs, clams, snails, worms, and other bottom animals.
size: Varies by species; some exceed 6 ft (1.8 m)
superpower: Permanent tooth plates work like nutcrackers on hard shells.
funFacts: Their skeleton is made of cartilage rather than bone.
Each side has one visible gill opening instead of a shark's several slits.
The upper jaw is fused directly to the skull.
Many chimeras carry a venomous defensive spine in front of the dorsal fin.
lookFor: Spot the large wing-like fins, rabbitish face, and whip-thin tail.

name: Gulper Eel
tagline: A pelican-sized mouth unfolds from a ribbon body.
intro: The gulper eel looks like a dark ribbon ending in an enormous scoop-shaped mouth. It can open that mouth wide and balloon its throat when food appears.
home: It drifts through tropical and temperate oceans worldwide, mostly 500 to 3,000 meters deep.
diet: It eats crustaceans, fishes, and cephalopods drifting through deep midwater.
size: Up to about 3.3 ft (1 m)—golf-club length
superpower: Its loose jaws and expandable throat turn into a giant living net.
funFacts: The lower jaw can make up about one-quarter of its total length.
A light-producing organ glows at the tip of its long tail.
Its scaleless skin is ultra-black and reflects very little light.
Despite the huge mouth, its teeth and eyes are quite small.
lookFor: Find the enormous pouch mouth, tiny eyes, and thread-like glowing tail.

name: Deep Sea Skate
tagline: A soft-winged hunter glides over the abyss.
intro: The deep sea skate seems to fly just above the ocean floor on broad fins. Its flattened body helps it search the mud without wasting much energy.
home: It lives on North Pacific seafloors about 360 to 2,900 meters deep.
diet: It hunts small fishes, crustaceans, worms, and other bottom animals.
size: Up to about 5.2 ft (1.6 m)—adult arm-span length
superpower: Sensitive pores detect the faint electrical signals made by hidden prey.
funFacts: Like sharks, skates have skeletons made of cartilage.
Skates lay their young inside tough egg cases sometimes called mermaid's purses.
Tiny tooth-like denticles roughen both sides of this skate's skin.
Its tail is longer than its body disc and ends with two small dorsal fins.
lookFor: Look for a pointed snout, diamond-like wings, and an extra-long narrow tail.

name: Goblin Shark
tagline: Its jaws launch forward like a spring trap.
intro: The goblin shark carries a long paddle-shaped snout and jaws that look too loose for its face. When prey comes near, those jaws shoot forward in a startling snap.
home: It follows continental slopes and seamounts worldwide, usually about 270 to 1,300 meters deep.
diet: It eats deep-water fishes, squid, and crustaceans.
size: Up to about 12.5 ft (3.8 m)—small-car length
superpower: Elastic jaw joints catapult the mouth forward to grab prey.
funFacts: Its pink color comes from blood vessels showing through pale translucent skin.
Electrosensory pores cover the long snout and help locate prey in darkness.
It is the only living member of the ancient shark family Mitsukurinidae.
Needle-like teeth near the front of the jaws snag soft, slippery animals.
lookFor: The flat blade-like snout and protruding pink jaws give it away.

name: Frilled Shark
tagline: Frilly gills frame a snake-shaped shark.
intro: The frilled shark winds through deep water with an eel-like body and a shark's toothy head. Its flexible jaws open wide to seize squid and other slippery prey.
home: It lives near continental slopes and canyons in scattered parts of the Atlantic and Pacific.
diet: It eats squid, bony fishes, and sometimes smaller sharks.
size: Up to about 6.6 ft (2 m)—taller than a doorway
superpower: A wide flexible gape may swallow prey about half the shark's length.
funFacts: Six pairs of feathery gill slits create the shark's frilled collar.
The first gill pair connects across the underside of the throat.
Rows of three-pronged teeth point backward to trap squid.
Its single small dorsal fin sits unusually far back near the tail.
lookFor: Find the long brown body, terminal mouth, and red-edged frilly gills.

name: Cookie Cutter
tagline: A tiny shark takes perfectly round bites.
intro: The cookiecutter shark is small enough to hold but bold enough to nibble giants. It suctions onto a passing animal, bites, and twists out a neat plug of flesh.
home: It spends days below 1,000 meters in warm oceans and rises toward the surface at night.
diet: It bites plugs from whales, seals, large fish, and sharks, and also eats small squid and crustaceans.
size: Up to about 22 in (56 cm)—about skateboard length
superpower: Suction-cup lips and saw-like lower teeth cut a round cookie-shaped bite.
funFacts: Glowing belly photophores help hide its silhouette from animals below.
A dark collar near the head may look like a tempting little fish.
It sheds its lower teeth as one connected row and swallows them to recycle calcium.
Cookiecutter bite marks have appeared on whales, sharks, and even submarines.
lookFor: Look for a cigar-shaped body, dark neck band, and wide round sucker mouth.

name: Megamouth Shark
tagline: A rare giant mouth follows krill through dim water.
intro: The Megamouth Shark is a slow-moving filter feeder with a huge rounded head and a surprisingly soft body. Scientists encounter it so rarely that each documented sighting adds valuable clues about its life.
home: Open ocean in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans, moving between shallow nighttime water and deeper daytime water.
diet: Mostly krill, plus copepods, jellyfish, and other small drifting animals.
size: At least 17 ft (5.5 m) - about the length of a small car
superpower: It pushes its jaws forward and expands its mouth to suck in plankton-rich water for filtering.
funFacts: The first known specimen was discovered in 1976 and required a new shark family, genus, and species.
It is one of only three giant filter-feeding shark species.
About fifty rows of tiny teeth line each jaw, but only a few rows are functional.
A tracked shark stayed shallow at night and descended more than 100 meters after dawn.
lookFor: Find the enormous front-facing mouth, rounded snout, dark back, and pale belly.

name: Giant Squid
tagline: Bus-sized tentacles reach through midnight water.
intro: The giant squid is a deep-sea legend made real, with eight arms and two extra-long feeding tentacles. Its enormous eyes watch for prey and approaching sperm whales in the gloom.
home: It lives in deep waters near continental and island slopes across the world's oceans.
diet: It grabs fishes, shrimp, and other squid with its feeding tentacles.
size: Largest recorded nearly 43 ft (13 m)—school-bus length
superpower: Eyes as wide as dinner plates gather tiny flashes of light.
funFacts: It has eight shorter arms plus two much longer feeding tentacles.
Rings of tiny teeth line the suckers on its tentacle clubs.
Sperm whales carry sucker scars and sometimes have giant-squid beaks in their stomachs.
Scientists first filmed a giant squid in its deep natural habitat in 2012.
lookFor: Count two very long tentacles beyond the eight arms and find the huge eyes.

name: Colossal Squid
tagline: The heavyweight squid carries swiveling hooks.
intro: The colossal squid is shorter-looking but much heavier than a giant squid. Thick arms and tentacles carry powerful hooks for gripping prey in icy Antarctic darkness.
home: It inhabits the deep Southern Ocean around Antarctica, often more than 1,000 meters down.
diet: It catches large fishes such as Antarctic toothfish and probably other squid.
size: Known specimen 14 ft (4.2 m) and 1,091 lb (495 kg)—small-car heavy
superpower: Swiveling hooks on its tentacle clubs turn to hold struggling prey.
funFacts: It is the heaviest invertebrate known to science.
Its eyes are the largest ever measured in an animal.
It is the only known squid with hooks that can rotate.
Circular scars and hard beaks reveal that sperm whales hunt colossal squid.
lookFor: Look for a thick red body, huge eyes, and hooks instead of only suckers.

name: Greenland Shark
tagline: An icy giant can outlive generations of humans.
intro: The Greenland shark cruises Arctic water at a wonderfully unhurried pace. Its cold, slow life may last for centuries, longer than any other known vertebrate.
home: It lives in cold Arctic and North Atlantic waters from the surface to great depths.
diet: It eats fishes, seals, and carrion found along the seafloor.
size: Usually 8–14 ft (2.4–4.3 m); giants may reach 24 ft (7.3 m)
superpower: A very slow metabolism helps it save energy and age extraordinarily slowly.
funFacts: One large female was estimated at about 392 years old, although the estimate has a wide range.
Greenland sharks grow only a tiny amount each year.
A small copepod often attaches to the surface of an eye.
Females give birth to live pups instead of laying egg cases.
lookFor: Notice the rounded snout, tiny fins, small eyes, and heavy gray body.

name: Giant Phantom Jelly
tagline: Four ghostly ribbons trail through the abyss.
intro: The giant phantom jelly drifts like a crimson umbrella with four enormous ribbons flowing behind. Scientists rarely meet this mysterious giant, even after thousands of deep-sea dives.
home: It appears in deep oceans worldwide except the Arctic, usually in the midnight zone.
diet: Scientists think it catches plankton and small fishes with its ribbon-like mouth arms.
size: Bell over 3.3 ft (1 m); arms longer than 33 ft (10 m)
superpower: Four curtain-like oral arms sweep a huge area without stinging tentacles.
funFacts: Unlike many jellies, it has no stinging tentacles around the bell.
Its deep crimson color looks almost black where sunlight never reaches.
MBARI has encountered only a handful during thousands of dives.
A small brotula fish has been seen hiding safely beside its giant bell.
lookFor: Find the broad dark-red bell and exactly four long flat trailing arms.

name: Deep Cucumber
tagline: A squishy recycler vacuums the ocean floor.
intro: Deep cucumbers are soft-bodied relatives of sea stars that creep across the mud. They swallow or sift old organic bits, turning leftovers into cleaner seafloor sediment.
home: Different species live on deep seafloors around the world.
diet: Most feed on detritus and tiny food particles in or above the mud.
size: Often around 8 in (20 cm), though species vary greatly
superpower: It recycles sunken leftovers and returns nutrients to the deep-sea food web.
funFacts: Sea cucumbers are echinoderms, the same major group as sea stars and urchins.
The feeding tentacles around the mouth are modified tube feet.
Tiny calcium pieces called ossicles support the otherwise soft body.
Some deep-sea species flap or paddle above the bottom instead of only crawling.
lookFor: Look for a soft cucumber-shaped body with feeding tentacles at one end.

name: Giant Red Shrimp
tagline: A crimson crustacean launches a glowing smoke screen.
intro: The giant red shrimp is really a giant lophogastrid, a shrimp-shaped kind of crustacean. Its deep crimson shell and clever chemistry suit the dark, low-oxygen ocean.
home: It occupies deep tropical and subtropical midwater in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans.
diet: It preys on smaller crustaceans and fishes.
size: Usually hand-sized; exceptional adults can reach 14 in (35 cm)
superpower: When threatened, it releases a glowing blue cloud that can confuse a hunter.
funFacts: It is a lophogastrid crustacean rather than a true decapod shrimp.
Red coloring appears nearly black in deep water, making useful camouflage.
Its oxygen-carrying hemocyanin works especially well where oxygen is scarce.
Like other lophogastrids, females protect developing young in a brood pouch.
lookFor: Spot the deep-red body, long pointed rostrum, and very long antennae.

name: Dumbo Octopus
tagline: Flappy ear-fins make deep-sea flight look easy.
intro: Dumbo octopuses flap two ear-like fins as they float above the seafloor. A web between their arms spreads like an umbrella when they steer or pounce.
home: They live on very deep seafloors worldwide, with some found beyond 4,000 meters.
diet: They swallow worms, snails, clams, crustaceans, and other small bottom animals.
size: Many are 8–12 in (20–30 cm)—about dinner-plate width
superpower: Gentle fin flaps provide energy-saving movement where food is scarce.
funFacts: This group includes some of the deepest-living octopuses ever observed.
The nickname comes from the flying-elephant ears of Disney's Dumbo.
Their arms connect with a broad web that can surround prey.
Females attach large eggs to hard surfaces such as deep-sea coral branches.
lookFor: Look for two rounded head fins and eight short arms joined by webbing.

name: Deep Sea Jelly
tagline: A blue pinwheel alarm summons bigger trouble.
intro: The deep sea jelly drifts like a dark-red saucer in the midnight zone. If attacked, it flashes a dazzling blue pinwheel that may call in an even larger predator.
home: It lives in deep waters worldwide, commonly about 500 to 5,000 meters down.
diet: It catches plankton, small crustaceans, and other drifting animals.
size: Up to about 6 in (15 cm)—small-plate width
superpower: Its bioluminescent burglar alarm may frighten attackers or attract their enemies.
funFacts: Red light vanishes quickly underwater, so its crimson bell looks black in the deep.
One tentacle grows much longer than the others and helps snag prey.
Blue light races around the bell in a spinning pattern when danger strikes.
A deep groove circles the bell and gives this group its crown-jelly nickname.
lookFor: Find the dark-red disk, crown-like groove, and one extra-long tentacle.

name: Peacock Squid
tagline: Glass skin, giant eyes, and lights underneath.
intro: The peacock squid belongs to a family nicknamed glass squids for their nearly transparent bodies. Giant eyes and carefully placed light organs help it watch and hide at the same time.
home: Species of Taonius drift through deep midwater in oceans around the world.
diet: It hunts fishes, crustaceans, and other small midwater animals.
size: Mantle up to about 26 in (66 cm), with arms and tentacles beyond
superpower: It can hold ink inside its body cavity to darken itself like a curtain.
funFacts: Peacock squids belong to the transparent glass-squid family Cranchiidae.
Their huge bulging eyes scan a wide area of dark water.
Photophores beneath the eyes shine downward and help erase the animal's shadow.
A clear body reveals internal organs that are packed into a compact central bundle.
lookFor: Look for a clear tapered body, bulbous eyes, and light organs below them.

name: Brittlestar
tagline: Five wriggly arms row across the seafloor.
intro: A brittlestar looks like a tiny center disk wearing five long snaky arms. It rows those flexible arms to scoot, climb, gather food, or escape danger.
home: Brittlestars live on seafloors worldwide, including deep mud, coral, sponges, and rocks.
diet: Different species catch drifting particles, scavenge scraps, or hunt tiny animals.
size: Often a coin-sized disk with arms five to eight times longer
superpower: It can drop a trapped arm and grow a replacement later.
funFacts: Brittlestars are echinoderm cousins of sea stars, urchins, and sea cucumbers.
About 2,000 living species are known.
Their arms bend at many little joints like a chain of vertebrae.
They move mainly by rowing their arms rather than walking on tube feet.
lookFor: Find a sharp-edged center disk with five clearly separate, snake-like arms.

name: Vampire Squid
tagline: A velvet cloak hides a gentle snow-eater.
intro: Despite its spooky name, the vampire squid does not suck blood or chase large prey. It gathers drifting marine snow with two long sticky feeding filaments.
home: It lives in low-oxygen deep water across tropical and temperate oceans.
diet: It eats marine snow made of tiny remains, mucus, molts, and waste.
size: Mantle up to about 12 in (30 cm)—ruler-length
superpower: It flips its webbed arms over its body to form a spiky defensive cloak.
funFacts: It is neither a true squid nor an octopus but the only living member of its family.
Its eyes are enormous compared with the size of its body.
The sticky feeding filaments can stretch to about eight times its body length.
Instead of ordinary ink, it can release glowing sticky mucus from its arm tips.
lookFor: Look for blue eyes, ear-like fins, and a dark web joining all eight arms.

name: Giant Isopod
tagline: A football-sized pillbug patrols the ocean floor.
intro: The giant isopod resembles a backyard pillbug scaled up to science-fiction size. It trundles across the deep seafloor searching for rare meals and falling leftovers.
home: It lives on deep Atlantic and Indo-West Pacific seafloors about 170 to 2,100 meters down.
diet: It scavenges dead fish and other remains and may also catch slow animals.
size: Up to about 16 in (40 cm)—roughly football length
superpower: Overlapping armor plates protect it and curl around its softer underside.
funFacts: Giant isopods are distant marine cousins of pillbugs and sowbugs.
Fourteen walking legs carry the heavy armored body.
Two pairs of antennae taste and feel through dark water.
Its extra-large size is an example of deep-sea gigantism.
lookFor: Spot the wide segmented armor, many legs, and large reflective compound eyes.

name: Giant Tube Worm
tagline: Friendly bacteria power a mouthless vent giant.
intro: The giant tube worm grows beside volcanic seafloor vents where poisonous-looking chemicals pour out. It has no mouth or stomach because bacteria living inside make all its food.
home: It forms colonies at hydrothermal vents in the eastern Pacific, about 1,900 to 3,600 meters deep.
diet: It does not eat; symbiotic bacteria make food from vent chemicals.
size: Up to about 6.6 ft (2 m)—taller than most adults
superpower: Billions of inner bacteria use chemosynthesis to turn chemicals into food.
funFacts: An adult has no mouth, gut, or anus.
Its red plume absorbs oxygen and hydrogen sulfide for the internal bacteria.
The worm snaps its soft plume inside the white tube when danger appears.
Free-swimming larvae help the species discover and settle newly formed vents.
lookFor: Look for a long white tube topped by a bright red feathery plume.

name: Oceanic Manta Ray
tagline: Giant wings follow the ocean's smallest meals.
intro: Oceanic manta rays are enormous filter feeders that migrate between rich feeding areas. Their broad fins carry them through open water while two head fins guide plankton toward their mouths.
home: Tropical, subtropical, and temperate seas worldwide, including offshore waters and productive coasts.
diet: Mostly tiny drifting animals such as copepods, krill, shrimp, and larvae.
size: Wingspan up to 26 ft (8 m), wider than two cars
superpower: Head fins form a funnel that carries plankton over filtering gill plates.
funFacts: Belly spot patterns help researchers recognize individual mantas.
Repeated somersaults keep a feeding manta inside a patch of plankton.
Usually solitary travelers, they also gather at cleaning and feeding sites.
Females typically produce one pup every two to three years.
lookFor: Look for a huge diamond-shaped body, broad wings, and two curled head fins.

name: Sardine Ball
tagline: A silver swirl that makes predators dizzy.
intro: A sardine ball is a tightly packed school of small, silvery fishes that turns almost like one giant animal. Sardine is a shared name for several members of the herring family, so this SeaPals creature represents the whole group.
home: Sardines gather in plankton-rich coastal and open waters around the world.
diet: They eat tiny plankton, including drifting animals and microscopic algae.
size: Usually 6-12 in (15-30 cm)—about ruler length
superpower: Thousands of neighbors can turn together in an instant and confuse attackers.
funFacts: Each fish follows nearby neighbors rather than a single school leader.
A dark back and pale belly camouflage sardines from above and below.
Sardines are important food for seabirds, marine mammals, and larger fishes.
Their lateral-line sensors detect vibrations and nearby movement in the water.
lookFor: Watch for a flashing silver cloud that ripples and changes shape.

name: Anchovy Ball
tagline: Tiny teammates with a giant place in the food web.
intro: An anchovy ball can contain thousands of slim fishes swirling shoulder to shoulder. The card's broad name covers the anchovy family, whose members connect microscopic plankton to much larger hunters.
home: Anchovies school near the surface in coastal and open waters worldwide.
diet: Most strain plankton from the water and also snap up tiny prey.
size: Usually 2-9 in (5-23 cm)—pencil to banana length
superpower: A crowded school makes it hard for a predator to choose one target.
funFacts: Anchovies often swim with their mouths open while gathering plankton.
Their upper jaw reaches behind the eye, unlike a sardine's shorter jaw.
Many anchovies live only a few years but reproduce in large numbers.
Healthy anchovy schools help feed tuna, whales, seabirds, and sea lions.
lookFor: Look for a slim silver fish with a large mouth and pointed snout.

name: Silverside Ball
tagline: A living ribbon of silver along the shore.
intro: SeaPals' silverside ball is represented by the Atlantic silverside, a little fish that gathers in glittering schools. Its bright side stripe can make the whole group flash when it turns.
home: Atlantic silversides live near beaches, inlets, and estuaries of eastern North America.
diet: They eat zooplankton, tiny crustaceans, algae, and small insect larvae.
size: Up to 7 in (18 cm)—about a new pencil
superpower: A mirror-bright stripe helps a turning school become a confusing flash.
funFacts: Atlantic silversides can handle both salty seawater and brackish estuaries.
They move into deeper offshore water when winter chills the coast.
Many coastal fishes and birds depend on silversides as prey.
Females attach sticky eggs to sand, gravel, or underwater plants.
lookFor: Find the bold silver stripe running down a slender, nearly see-through body.

name: Herring Ball
tagline: Millions of silver swimmers keep northern seas humming.
intro: Atlantic herring travel in enormous schools that can shimmer across the water. These small fish are a mighty link between plankton and ocean predators.
home: They roam cool North Atlantic coastal and continental-shelf waters.
diet: They eat zooplankton, krill, and drifting fish larvae.
size: Up to 14 in (36 cm)—a little longer than a ruler
superpower: Coordinated migrations lead whole schools between feeding, spawning, and wintering grounds.
funFacts: A female can release tens of thousands of eggs in one season.
Herring eggs can carpet rocky or gravelly seafloor in thick patches.
They may live for about 15 years, surprisingly long for a small fish.
Whales, sharks, cod, seabirds, and seals all hunt Atlantic herring.
lookFor: Look for a blue-green back, silver sides, and a deeply forked tail.

name: Krill Bloom
tagline: Tiny crustaceans that power some of Earth's biggest animals.
intro: A krill bloom is a dense swarm of shrimp-like crustaceans, not a patch of flowers. Packed together by the thousands, krill become an ocean feast big enough for giant whales.
home: Different krill species swarm in oceans worldwide, from polar seas to the tropics.
diet: They graze on phytoplankton and also eat other tiny drifting organisms.
size: Most 0.4-2.4 in (1-6 cm)—paper-clip to finger length
superpower: Synchronized swarms concentrate tiny meals into whale-sized mouthfuls.
funFacts: Krill are crustaceans, making them relatives of crabs and shrimp.
Many krill species have light-making organs called photophores.
They shed their outer skeleton as they grow and can even shrink when food is scarce.
Fish, penguins, seals, seabirds, and baleen whales all eat krill.
lookFor: Look for a nearly transparent, shrimp-shaped body with feathery swimming legs.

name: Bluefin Tuna
tagline: A warm-powered athlete built to cross an ocean.
intro: Atlantic bluefin tuna are torpedo-shaped travelers with muscles made for speed and endurance. Juveniles grow from school-sized hunters into some of the largest bony fish in the Atlantic.
home: They migrate across the Atlantic between rich feeding waters and warm spawning areas.
diet: They hunt fishes, squid, and crustaceans, with prey changing as they grow.
size: Up to about 10 ft (3 m) and 1,000 lb (450 kg)—motorcycle-heavy
superpower: Special heat exchangers keep their swimming muscles warmer than the surrounding sea.
funFacts: Bluefin can cross the Atlantic and later return to familiar spawning regions.
Grooves let them tuck in several fins to reduce drag while swimming.
They must keep water flowing over their gills as they cruise.
Tiny finlets behind the main fins help smooth fast-moving water around the body.
lookFor: Spot a thick, streamlined body with a dark blue back and short yellow finlets.

name: Swordfish
tagline: A deep-diving hunter with a built-in sword and heater.
intro: Swordfish sweep their flattened bills through schools of prey, stunning or injuring meals before swallowing them. They race between warm surface water and chilly depths in oceans around the globe.
home: They range through tropical, temperate, and sometimes cold waters worldwide.
diet: They eat schooling fishes, squid, and other open-water animals.
size: Up to 15 ft (4.6 m) and over 1,000 lb (450 kg)—small-car weight
superpower: A special heater keeps their eyes and brain warm during cold, deep dives.
funFacts: The sword is a flattened upper jaw, not a nose horn.
Adults lose the teeth and rough scales they had when young.
Females grow larger than males and can release millions of eggs.
Swordfish usually travel alone rather than in tight schools.
lookFor: Find the long flat bill, crescent tail, and tall curved front fin.

name: Black Marlin
tagline: A heavyweight billfish with fins that never fold flat.
intro: Black marlin are massive, muscular billfish of the Indo-Pacific. They slash at swift prey with a stout bill and then gulp the stunned animals.
home: They patrol tropical and subtropical Pacific and Indian Ocean waters.
diet: They hunt tuna, mackerel, trevallies, squid, and other fast swimmers.
size: Over 14 ft (4.4 m) and 1,500 lb (700 kg)—grand-piano weight
superpower: A powerful tail launches rapid attacks on prey built for speed.
funFacts: Unlike other marlins, a black marlin cannot fold its stiff pectoral fins flat.
Its second dorsal fin sits slightly ahead of its second anal fin.
The body is dark blue above and silvery below, usually without bold stripes.
A few individuals round southern Africa and wander into the Atlantic.
lookFor: Check for rigid side fins sticking out from a deep, dark-backed body.

name: Shortfin Mako Shark
tagline: A warm-muscled shark shaped like a living rocket.
intro: Shortfin makos are sleek open-ocean sharks famous for sudden speed and long migrations. Their metallic blue bodies slice through temperate and tropical seas.
home: Adults roam offshore waters worldwide while juveniles often use coastal areas.
diet: They eat squid, tuna, bluefish, swordfish, and other sharks.
size: Up to about 13 ft (4 m)—longer than a small car
superpower: Heat exchangers warm key muscles so they can chase fast prey efficiently.
funFacts: Long pointed teeth remain visible even when the mouth is closed.
Females give birth to live pups after the young develop inside them.
Some tagged makos travel across entire ocean basins.
Young makos may be hunted by larger sharks and killer whales.
lookFor: Look for a sharp cone-shaped snout, big dark eyes, and metallic-blue back.

name: Sperm Whale
tagline: The biggest toothed whale hunts by sound in darkness.
intro: Sperm whales dive into deep, dark water and search with powerful clicks. Their enormous square heads hold the sound-focusing organs that make this hunt possible.
home: They live in deep oceans worldwide, from the equator toward polar ice.
diet: They mainly hunt squid and deep-water fishes, including some large squid.
size: Females about 40 ft; males to 52 ft (12-16 m)—school-bus length
superpower: Extremely powerful echolocation clicks reveal prey far beyond the reach of sunlight.
funFacts: Sperm whales are the largest members of the toothed-whale group.
Their single blowhole sits left of center, making a low angled spout.
They often lift their tail flukes before beginning a deep dive.
Females and young live in social groups while mature males often travel separately.
lookFor: Notice the huge blocky head, wrinkled gray skin, and angled blow.

name: Pilot Whale
tagline: Deep-diving dolphins that stick close to their families.
intro: Pilot whale is the shared name for two very social dolphin species with rounded foreheads. Both travel in close family pods and use echolocation to chase prey below the light.
home: They favor deep temperate or tropical waters, often near continental slopes.
diet: They mostly hunt squid and fishes, especially during deep nighttime dives.
size: About 13-25 ft (4-7.6 m), depending on species and sex
superpower: Family pods coordinate in darkness using whistles, clicks, and excellent echolocation.
funFacts: Pilot whales are large dolphins, despite having whale in their name.
Long-finned and short-finned pilot whales are very hard to distinguish at sea.
Many pods are centered on related females and stay together for years.
They sometimes rest at the surface in side-by-side rows.
lookFor: Look for a dark body, bulbous forehead, and broad backswept dorsal fin.

name: Killer Whale
tagline: Ocean families turn teamwork into top-predator power.
intro: Killer whales are the largest dolphins and among the ocean's most skilled hunters. Different communities pass down their own calls, travel routes, and hunting traditions.
home: They live in every ocean, from polar seas to warm tropical water.
diet: Diet depends on the community and may include fish, squid, sharks, or marine mammals.
size: About 20-32 ft (6-9.8 m)—up to bus length
superpower: Pods teach and coordinate specialized hunting plans across generations.
funFacts: Each pod has a recognizable collection of calls, rather like a dialect.
Mothers and their grown offspring may remain together for life.
The gray saddle patch behind the dorsal fin differs among individuals.
Wild killer whales have no regular natural predator once fully grown.
lookFor: Spot bold black-and-white coloring and a tall fin behind a gray saddle patch.

name: Basking Shark
tagline: A gentle giant swims with a mouth like a tunnel.
intro: Basking sharks cruise slowly with huge mouths open, filtering clouds of plankton from seawater. Their size looks startling, but their tiny prey is barely bigger than a crumb.
home: They migrate through cool and temperate coastal and offshore waters worldwide.
diet: They filter zooplankton, fish eggs, and tiny larvae using comb-like gill rakers.
size: Often 20-26 ft; up to about 33 ft (6-10 m)—bus length
superpower: Enormous gill slits strain plankton from a nonstop river of seawater.
funFacts: The basking shark is the second-largest living fish after the whale shark.
It is one of only three giant filter-feeding shark species.
The name comes from sightings of sharks appearing to bask near the surface.
Basking sharks sometimes leap completely out of the water.
lookFor: Look for a huge open mouth, pointed snout, and gill slits circling the head.

name: Humpback Whale
tagline: A singing traveler with wings and bubble-made fishing nets.
intro: Humpback whales migrate thousands of miles between feeding and breeding waters. They are acrobatic baleen whales whose songs, breaches, and extra-long flippers make them ocean standouts.
home: They live in every ocean and migrate between cold feeding grounds and warmer nurseries.
