diet: They gulp krill and small schooling fishes, filtering food through baleen.
size: Up to about 60 ft (18 m) and 40 tons—city-bus length
superpower: Some humpbacks blow spirals of bubbles that crowd fish into a gulpable bundle.
funFacts: Their pectoral flippers can reach about one-third of the whale's body length.
Males sing long, changing song patterns during breeding season.
The bumps on a humpback's head contain sensory hairs.
Scientists identify individuals using the unique markings under their tail flukes.
lookFor: Watch for knobby head bumps, very long white-edged flippers, and a humped dive.

name: Blue Whale
tagline: Earth's largest animal lives on bite-sized krill.
intro: Blue whales are the largest animals known to have lived, yet they feed mostly on tiny crustaceans. A long, streamlined body carries them across vast ocean feeding and breeding ranges.
home: They roam oceans worldwide, often following seasonal patches of krill.
diet: They lunge through dense krill swarms and strain each mouthful through baleen.
size: Up to about 100 ft (30 m) and 200 tons—three buses long
superpower: Expandable throat pleats let one lunge capture an enormous volume of krill-filled water.
funFacts: Mottled gray skin appears bright blue when seen through seawater.
Their tall, straight blow can rise more than 20 feet into the air.
Low blue-whale calls can travel huge distances through the ocean.
A newborn calf drinks rich milk and gains weight extremely quickly.
lookFor: Look for a very long blue-gray back and a tiny dorsal fin far behind.

name: Whale Shark
tagline: The world's biggest fish wears a starry fingerprint.
intro: Whale sharks are gentle, bus-sized sharks that filter tiny food from warm seas. Every individual carries a unique constellation of pale spots and stripes.
home: They wander tropical and warm-temperate oceans, often gathering where food blooms.
diet: They filter plankton, fish eggs, small fishes, crustaceans, and squid.
size: Commonly to 40 ft (12 m), with larger records—school-bus length
superpower: Filtering pads inside the gills sift tiny prey from huge mouthfuls of water.
funFacts: The whale shark is the largest living fish, not a whale.
Its broad mouth opens near the front of its flat head.
Researchers identify individuals by spot patterns, much like human fingerprints.
Whale sharks can dive thousands of feet below their usual surface feeding areas.
lookFor: Find a broad flat head and a dark back covered in pale spots and bars.

name: Ocean Sunfish
tagline: A giant swimming pancake with no ordinary tail.
intro: Ocean sunfish look like an enormous fish whose tail was neatly erased. They roam widely, diving for gelatinous prey and returning toward the sunlit surface.
home: They live across tropical and temperate oceans around the globe.
diet: They eat jellies, salps, squid, crustaceans, small fishes, and algae.
size: Up to about 10 ft (3 m) and over 2,000 lb (900 kg)—car-sized
superpower: Powerful dorsal and anal fins flap together to propel the tailless-looking body.
funFacts: The rounded rear edge is a rudder-like structure called a clavus.
Newly hatched sunfish are tiny, round, and spiny like their pufferfish relatives.
Dozens of parasite species may live on or inside one ocean sunfish.
They sometimes bask near the surface after feeding in colder deep water.
lookFor: Look for a tall, flattened disk with towering fins and a scalloped rear edge.

name: Flying Fish
tagline: A fin-winged escape artist that glides above the waves.
intro: Flying fish do not flap through the sky like birds; they launch from the sea and glide. Oversized fins turn a high-speed escape from predators into a breathtaking flight.
home: More than 40 species live near the surface of warm oceans worldwide.
diet: They eat plankton, small crustaceans, and other tiny drifting food.
size: Most under 12 in; some to 18 in (46 cm)—about a skateboard
superpower: Wing-like fins carry a speeding fish hundreds of feet above the water.
funFacts: The longer lower half of the tail provides the final push for takeoff.
Some species have enlarged pelvic fins and seem to have four wings.
Flying fish may touch the tail back down and relaunch without ending a glide.
Their eggs often have sticky threads that cling to floating material.
lookFor: Watch for a torpedo-shaped fish with enormous pointed pectoral fins.

name: Halfbeak
tagline: A surface skimmer with only half a long beak.
intro: Halfbeaks are slim schooling fishes whose lower jaw stretches far beyond the upper jaw. They cruise just under warm ocean surfaces and become meals for many larger hunters.
home: Marine halfbeaks school near the surface of tropical and subtropical seas.
diet: They nibble algae, plankton, small crustaceans, and other surface morsels.
size: Most 7-18 in (18-46 cm)—forearm length
superpower: Tight surface schools can sprint and leap away from approaching predators.
funFacts: Their family name means half-beak, describing the much longer lower jaw.
Halfbeaks are close relatives of flying fishes and needlefishes.
Billfish, tuna, wahoo, sharks, and dolphins all hunt them.
Many species lay eggs with threads that fasten to floating or underwater plants.
lookFor: Spot the long lower jaw beneath a much shorter triangular upper jaw.

name: Needlefish
tagline: A surface hunter armed with a beakful of needles.
intro: Needlefishes are long, narrow hunters with both jaws stretched into a toothy beak. They stalk small prey near the surface and can leap when startled.
home: The family lives in tropical and temperate seas worldwide, with some freshwater species.
diet: They grab small fishes, squid, and swimming crustaceans with sharp teeth.
size: Many 1-3 ft (30-90 cm); the largest approach 5 ft (1.5 m)
superpower: A slim body can burst forward almost invisibly along the bright surface.
funFacts: Needlefish have many fine teeth lining both elongated jaws.
Their dorsal and anal fins sit far back near the tail.
The bones of many needlefish have a harmless greenish color.
Young needlefish begin life with shorter jaws that lengthen as they grow.
lookFor: Look for a pencil-thin body and two equally long, toothy jaws.

name: Barracuda
tagline: A silver ambush rocket with a mouthful of daggers.
intro: SeaPals' barracuda is represented by the great barracuda, a watchful hunter with a long torpedo body. It waits, aims by sight, and bursts forward before prey can react.
home: Great barracudas use tropical reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, and nearby open water.
diet: They hunt fishes, including jacks, grunts, snappers, herrings, and small tuna.
size: Commonly 2-4 ft; up to about 6.5 ft (2 m)—adult-height
superpower: A flexible backbone and powerful tail produce lightning-fast ambush sprints.
funFacts: Two sets of sharp teeth slice prey or hold it firmly.
Black spots on the lower sides help identify a great barracuda.
Young fish shelter among mangrove roots and seagrass before moving deeper.
Adults are often solitary, while young barracudas may gather in groups.
lookFor: Find a pointed snout, jutting lower jaw, dark spots, and widely separated back fins.

name: Remora
tagline: The ocean's hitchhiker carries its own suction cup.
intro: Remoras ride sharks, rays, turtles, whales, and even boats using a gripping disk on the head. The SeaPals card represents a family of eight specialized hitchhiking species.
home: Most remoras travel through warm open oceans wherever large hosts roam.
diet: They eat plankton, scraps, small animals, and sometimes parasites from a host.
size: About 1-3 ft (30-90 cm)—ruler to baseball-bat length
superpower: A modified dorsal fin forms a ridged disk that grips without biting.
funFacts: The suction disk began as the same kind of fin found on other fishes' backs.
A remora can slide backward to release its grip and swim away.
The free ride saves energy and carries the fish toward fresh feeding opportunities.
Different remora species favor hosts such as sharks, billfish, mantas, or whales.
lookFor: Look for a flat, striped oval disk on top of the head.

name: Mahi-Mahi
tagline: A rainbow-fast fish that grows almost while you watch.
intro: Mahi-mahi blaze through warm oceans in electric blue, green, gold, and silver. These tireless hunters grow at an astonishing pace and often search beneath floating Sargassum.
home: They roam tropical and subtropical waters in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans.
diet: They chase flying fish, squid, crustaceans, and many other open-water animals.
size: Up to about 6.8 ft (2.1 m), though most are smaller
superpower: Exceptionally fast growth can produce a four-foot fish in its first year.
funFacts: Mahi-mahi are fishes and are not related to marine-mammal dolphins.
A single dorsal fin runs almost the entire length of the body.
Mature males develop a tall, nearly vertical forehead.
Their brilliant colors fade quickly after the fish dies.
lookFor: Spot a blunt head, long continuous back fin, and glowing blue-green-gold colors.

name: Bluefish
tagline: A schooling hunter with serious teeth and endless energy.
intro: Bluefish are fierce, fast-moving hunters that chase prey in churning schools. Their worldwide travels follow comfortable water and abundant baitfish.
home: They inhabit temperate and subtropical coastal and offshore waters in many oceans.
diet: They eat schooling fishes, squid, and crustaceans.
size: Usually 1-2 ft; up to about 4 ft (1.2 m)—child-height
superpower: Whole schools cooperate to herd and rush tightly packed prey.
funFacts: Bluefish have one row of sharp, closely spaced teeth in each jaw.
Small young bluefish are often nicknamed snappers.
Their forked tails and sturdy bodies are built for strong swimming.
Only one living species belongs to the bluefish family Pomatomidae.
lookFor: Look for a blue-green back, silver sides, forked tail, and toothy mouth.

name: Bonito Tuna
tagline: A striped speedster from the tuna-and-mackerel family.
intro: SeaPals' bonito tuna is the Atlantic bonito, a compact relative of tuna and mackerel. It races in schools through Atlantic and Mediterranean waters after small fish.
home: Atlantic bonito use warm and temperate coastal waters of the Atlantic and nearby seas.
diet: They swallow small schooling fishes such as mackerel, menhaden, and sand lance.
size: Up to about 3 ft (90 cm)—baseball-bat length
superpower: A torpedo body and stabilizing finlets support rapid, sustained pursuit.
funFacts: Dark diagonal stripes run along the upper back rather than the belly.
Bonito have small sharp teeth, unlike many similarly shaped tuna.
They must swallow prey whole because their jaws are built for grabbing, not chewing.
Larger tuna, marlin, wahoo, and sharks hunt Atlantic bonito.
lookFor: Find several dark slanting stripes across a blue-green back.

name: King Mackerel
tagline: A sleek silver king that chases schools at speed.
intro: King mackerel are long, powerful fishes that migrate with warm coastal water. Their fins tuck into grooves while rows of little finlets steady a high-speed chase.
home: They range along the western Atlantic from the Americas into the Gulf and Caribbean.
diet: They mainly hunt schooling fishes and also eat squid and shrimp.
size: Often 20-35 in; up to 6 ft (1.8 m)—adult-height
superpower: Streamlined fins fold into grooves to reduce drag during a sprint.
funFacts: Young king mackerel have bronze spots that usually fade with age.
A sharply dropping lateral line helps distinguish them from similar mackerels.
Females can grow larger and live longer than males.
Thirty triangular teeth form an efficient fish-grabbing row.
lookFor: Check for a silvery body, sharply dipping side line, and tiny rear finlets.

name: Crevalle Jack
tagline: A hard-pulling jack that thrives from rivers to reefs.
intro: Crevalle jacks are powerful schooling fishes with broad chests and deeply forked tails. They can handle an unusual range of water, from the open sea into salty rivers.
home: They live in western Atlantic coastal waters, estuaries, reefs, and offshore areas.
diet: They hunt fishes, shrimp, crabs, and other swimming animals.
size: Usually about 2 ft; up to 3.3 ft (1 m)—yardstick length
superpower: A flexible tolerance for salinity lets them hunt from sea to river water.
funFacts: A dark oval blotch marks the base of each pectoral fin.
The chest is mostly scaleless except for a small central patch.
Young crevalle jacks have vertical bars that fade as they mature.
Large adults sometimes travel alone, but most form energetic schools.
lookFor: Look for a black gill-cover spot, pectoral-fin blotch, and deeply forked yellowish tail.

name: Yellowtail Amberjack
tagline: A golden-striped traveler with a powerful forked tail.
intro: Yellowtail amberjacks are strong, migratory jacks that patrol coastal and offshore water. A bright yellow side stripe points toward the tail that powers their chase.
home: They occur in subtropical and temperate seas, especially in the Southern Hemisphere.
diet: They hunt fishes, squid, and crustaceans around reefs and open water.
size: Often around 4 ft; exceptionally over 6 ft (1.8 m)—adult-height
superpower: A muscular body and deeply forked tail deliver long-distance speed.
funFacts: Young yellowtails often school, while large adults may roam in smaller groups.
The yellow stripe runs straight from the snout toward the tail.
They gather near rocky reefs, offshore islands, and floating objects.
The name yellowtail is used for several regional relatives, which can cause confusion.
lookFor: Find the straight yellow side stripe and matching golden, deeply forked tail.

name: African Pompano
tagline: Youngsters trail silver streamers like underwater kites.
intro: African pompano change dramatically as they grow from ribbon-finned drifters into powerful silver adults. Despite the name, they circle warm seas around the world, not only Africa.
home: Young fish drift offshore while adults patrol tropical coastal seas and reefs.
diet: They eat fishes, squid, and crustaceans.
size: Usually under 3 ft; up to about 5 ft (1.5 m)—child-height
superpower: Extra-long juvenile fin streamers may make a young fish harder to target.
funFacts: Juvenile dorsal and anal fin rays trail far beyond the body.
The dramatic streamers shorten as the fish becomes an adult.
Tiny embedded scales make an adult's silver body look almost scaleless.
A small dark blotch sits near the upper edge of the gill opening.
lookFor: Look for a deep silver body; youngsters carry extremely long ribbon-like fins.

name: Frigate Tuna
tagline: A small tuna built for warm-water sprints.
intro: Frigate tuna are compact, fast schooling relatives of larger tuna. They chase small prey near the surface throughout tropical and subtropical oceans.
home: They roam warm offshore and coastal waters around the world.
diet: They eat small fishes, squid, and planktonic crustaceans.
size: Usually 1-2 ft; up to about 2.1 ft (65 cm)—arm length
superpower: Rows of finlets and a narrow tail base stabilize rapid swimming.
funFacts: Wavy dark markings cover the back behind the front dorsal fin.
The belly and lower sides are plain silvery white.
Frigate tuna often form schools with other small tuna species.
They are both hunters and important prey for billfish, sharks, and larger tuna.
lookFor: Spot wavy dark back stripes, a bare silver belly, and tiny rear finlets.

name: Lookdown
tagline: Turn sideways and this silver fish nearly disappears.
intro: Lookdowns are deep-bodied silver jacks compressed almost as thin as dinner plates. Their strange sloping foreheads and mirror-like sides make them masters of changing visibility.
home: They school in warm western Atlantic coastal waters, bays, and estuaries.
diet: They pick small fishes, shrimp, crabs, and worms from the water and seafloor.
size: Up to about 19 in (48 cm)—roughly skateboard length
superpower: A paper-thin body can reflect light or vanish when turned edge-on.
funFacts: Adults have an extremely steep, angular forehead above a low mouth.
Tiny embedded scales make the body look smooth and almost scaleless.
Young lookdowns trail long fin rays that shorten as they grow.
Lookdowns belong to the jack family alongside pompano and amberjacks.
lookFor: Find the shiny, wafer-thin body with a steep forehead and long curved fins.

name: Pompano
tagline: A silver beach cruiser that digs up crunchy snacks.
intro: SeaPals' pompano is represented by the Florida pompano, a quick silver jack of sandy coasts. It darts through surf and shallow bays searching for hard-shelled morsels.
home: Florida pompano live over sandy beaches, bays, and estuaries of the western Atlantic.
diet: They eat clams, snails, shrimp, crabs, worms, and small fishes.
size: Up to about 25 in (64 cm)—a little over two rulers
superpower: Strong throat plates crush the shells of small clams and crustaceans.
funFacts: Adults may lose the tiny jaw teeth they had when young.
A deeply forked tail drives fast swimming through breaking surf.
Their plain silver bodies are blue-green above and white below.
Pompano eggs and larvae drift freely in the plankton.
lookFor: Look for a smooth silver body, blunt snout, yellowish fins, and forked tail.

name: Ocean Triggerfish
tagline: A tough-skinned drifter with a lockable fin trigger.
intro: Ocean triggerfish are sturdy, deep-bodied fishes that roam warm open water and gather near floating objects. A locking spine on the back gives the whole triggerfish family its name.
home: They occur across warm Atlantic open water, reefs, and floating Sargassum communities.
diet: They eat zooplankton, small crustaceans, mollusks, and other drifting animals.
size: Up to about 26 in (65 cm)—roughly two rulers long
superpower: The first dorsal spine locks upright until a smaller trigger spine releases it.
funFacts: Thick, leathery skin is covered in rough diagonal scale plates.
Each jaw has eight strong outer teeth for crunching tough food.
The pelvic fins are reduced to a small set of armored-looking scales.
Young ocean triggerfish often shelter beneath floating seaweed or debris.
lookFor: Spot a dark gray, deep body with a black patch at the pectoral-fin base.

name: Tripletail
tagline: A sideways leaf disguise hides three pretend tails.
intro: Tripletails often float on their sides near seaweed or debris, pretending to be a drifting leaf. Rounded rear fins frame the real tail and create the illusion of three tails.
home: They use tropical and subtropical bays, estuaries, offshore water, and floating cover worldwide.
diet: They ambush small fishes, shrimp, crabs, and other crustaceans.
size: Up to about 3.6 ft (1.1 m)—baseball-bat length
superpower: Sideways leaf mimicry lets a patient hunter drift close to unsuspecting prey.
funFacts: The soft dorsal and anal fins look like two extra rounded tails.
Juveniles may be yellow, mottled, or dark brown like floating leaves.
Young tripletails often shelter in drifting Sargassum.
They can tolerate both full seawater and brackish estuaries.
lookFor: Look for a leaf-like fish floating sideways beside a buoy, log, or seaweed.

name: Blue Sea Dragon
tagline: A tiny upside-down dragon steals stings from its lunch.
intro: Blue sea dragons are floating sea slugs that ride the ocean surface upside down. They eat stinging animals and save some unfired stinging cells for their own defense.
home: They drift at the surface of tropical and temperate oceans around the world.
diet: They prey on Portuguese man o' wars, blue buttons, and other floating relatives.
size: Usually under 2 in (5 cm)—about thumb length
superpower: Stolen stinging cells are stored in finger-like tips and reused against attackers.
funFacts: A swallowed air bubble in the stomach helps the slug stay afloat.
It floats belly-up, so its blue side faces skyward and silver side faces downward.
Each blue sea dragon has both male and female reproductive organs.
Its stored stings can still hurt people, so stranded animals should not be touched.
lookFor: Find a tiny silver-blue slug with six clusters of feathery, finger-like arms.

name: Man O' War
tagline: A floating colony sails with a curtain of stingers.
intro: A Portuguese man o' war is not one jellyfish but a colony of specialized animals called zooids. A gas-filled float catches the wind while long tentacles fish below.
home: It drifts on the surface of warm Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean waters.
diet: Stinging tentacles capture fish larvae, small fishes, shrimp, and other plankton.
size: Float to about 12 in (30 cm); tentacles can trail over 30 ft (9 m)
superpower: Thousands of stinging capsules fire microscopic venom threads on contact.
funFacts: Different zooids handle floating, feeding, defense, or reproduction for the colony.
The colony cannot swim and travels mainly with wind and currents.
Some floats lean left and others right, spreading colonies in different directions.
Detached or beached tentacles may still sting and should never be touched.
lookFor: Watch for a blue-purple gas float shaped like a tiny translucent sailboat.

name: Market Squid
tagline: An iridescent jet swimmer with a one-year adventure.
intro: Market squid flicker with changing color as huge schools cruise the Pacific coast. Near the end of their short lives, adults gather over sandy seafloor to lay forests of egg capsules.
home: They range through eastern Pacific coastal water from Mexico toward southeastern Alaska.
diet: They eat small fishes, crustaceans, and marine worms.
size: Up to about 11 in (28 cm)—roughly ruler length
superpower: A muscular mantle blasts water through a funnel for rapid jet propulsion.
funFacts: Market squid grow quickly and usually live for only about one year.
Skin cells called chromatophores create fast-changing patterns and signals.
Each torpedo-shaped egg capsule can hold roughly 180 to 300 eggs.
Adults usually die after the great spawning gatherings.
lookFor: Look for a slender opalescent body, two triangular fins, eight arms, and two tentacles.

name: Wahoo
tagline: Blue racing stripes mark one of the sea's sprinters.
intro: Wahoo are long, toothy ocean predators built for explosive pursuits. Bright cobalt bars flash against silver sides as they rush down fast prey.
home: They roam tropical and subtropical oceans, often near islands or drifting objects.
diet: They eat tuna, flying fish, mahi-mahi, squid, jacks, and other open-water prey.
size: Usually 3-5.5 ft; up to about 8 ft (2.5 m)—door-height or longer
superpower: A streamlined body can burst to roughly 47 mph (75 km/h).
funFacts: Wahoo usually travel alone or in small, loose groups.
Twenty-four or more wavy cobalt bars cross their sides.
Finlets behind the dorsal and anal fins steady the fish at speed.
Their beak-like jaws hold finely serrated triangular teeth.
lookFor: Find a very long silver body crossed by many electric-blue vertical bars.

name: Yellowfin Tuna
tagline: Golden fins slice warm oceans at marathon speed.
intro: Yellowfin tuna are powerful open-ocean hunters named for their glowing yellow fins and finlets. Schools travel through warm seas, sometimes alongside dolphins or other tuna.
home: They live throughout tropical and subtropical Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean waters.
diet: They hunt fishes, squid, octopus, shrimp, and swimming crabs.
size: Up to about 7 ft (2.1 m) and 400 lb (180 kg)—motorcycle-heavy
superpower: A warm swimming core and streamlined body support fast, tireless travel.
funFacts: Large adults grow long, sickle-shaped second dorsal and anal fins.
A metallic yellow stripe runs along each side.
Rows of bright finlets guide water smoothly toward the crescent tail.
Females release eggs in batches, often spawning repeatedly in warm water.
lookFor: Look for a dark-blue back, yellow side stripe, golden finlets, and crescent tail.

name: Sailfish
tagline: A color-changing sail helps herd dinner into reach.
intro: Sailfish carry a spectacular dorsal fin that towers above the body like a sail. Working alone or together, they corral schooling prey and slash with their long bills.
home: They roam tropical and subtropical Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Ocean waters.
diet: They eat sardines, anchovies, mackerel, jacks, squid, and other schooling prey.
size: Up to about 11 ft (3.4 m), including the bill—small-car length
superpower: The huge sail flashes color and helps fence nervous prey into a tight group.
funFacts: The sail can fold into a groove to reduce drag while cruising.
Its bill stuns or injures prey with quick sideways slashes.
Body bars can brighten when a sailfish is excited or hunting.
Young sailfish can grow more than four feet long in their first year.
lookFor: Spot a long round bill and an enormous dark-blue sail dotted with black.

name: Blue Shark
tagline: Long-winged and bright blue, this shark never stops roaming.
intro: Blue sharks are graceful open-ocean wanderers with exceptionally long pectoral fins. Their cobalt backs fade to brilliant white bellies, perfect camouflage in deep blue water.
home: They cross temperate and tropical oceans, often following cooler water and prey.
diet: They mainly eat squid and fishes, plus cuttlefish, octopuses, and crustaceans.
size: Commonly 6-9 ft; up to about 12 ft (3.8 m)—small-car length
superpower: Extra-long pectoral fins provide efficient lift during enormous ocean journeys.
funFacts: Blue sharks make some of the longest migrations recorded for sharks.
They often hunt squid at night when the prey rises toward the surface.
Females give birth to live pups, sometimes in very large litters.
The pointed snout and slender body are more delicate-looking than many requiem sharks.
lookFor: Look for a vivid blue back, narrow snout, and remarkably long side fins.

name: Galapagos Shark
tagline: An island-patrolling shark with a curious streak.
intro: Galapagos sharks gather around far-flung oceanic islands in warm seas worldwide. They are bold, inquisitive hunters that resemble dusky sharks so closely even experts check carefully.
home: They favor clear tropical water around islands, reefs, and continental shelves.
diet: Young sharks eat bottom fishes; adults add rays, squid, octopuses, and smaller sharks.
size: Up to about 11 ft (3.3 m)—small-car length
superpower: Sensitive smell and electroreception help locate prey around dark island slopes.
funFacts: The species was first described from the waters around the Galápagos Islands.
Females give birth to live pups after embryos develop inside them.
Young sharks often use shallower island water as a nursery.
Experts may count backbone vertebrae to separate this species from a dusky shark.
lookFor: Find a tall first dorsal fin, rounded snout, gray-brown back, and white belly.

name: Oceanic Whitetip Shark
tagline: White-tipped paddle fins cruise the far open sea.
intro: Oceanic whitetips patrol warm blue water far from shore on broad, rounded fins. They conserve energy while cruising, then investigate promising scents or splashes with persistence.
home: They live near the surface of tropical and subtropical open oceans worldwide.
diet: They eat tuna, squid, stingrays, sea turtles, seabirds, and carrion.
size: Usually 6-10 ft; exceptionally near 13 ft (4 m)—small-car length
superpower: Wide wing-like fins make long-distance open-ocean cruising remarkably efficient.
funFacts: The first dorsal, pectoral, and tail fins have rounded white-marked tips.
Pilot fish and remoras often travel beside these sharks.
They spend much more time offshore than the similarly named whitetip reef shark.
Females nourish developing pups internally and give birth to live young.
lookFor: Look for very broad rounded fins with white tips and a blunt snout.

name: Silky Shark
tagline: Tiny tooth-like scales give this shark a silky glide.
intro: Silky sharks are slender warm-water hunters named for unusually smooth-feeling skin. They travel the open ocean around tuna schools, seamounts, and islands.
home: They inhabit tropical oceans, from offshore surface water to deeper continental slopes.
diet: They hunt tuna, mackerel, sardines, squid, octopuses, and crustaceans.
size: Usually 6-8 ft; up to about 11 ft (3.3 m)—small-car length
superpower: Densely packed, tiny skin denticles reduce roughness and inspire the silky name.
funFacts: The first dorsal fin begins behind the rear tip of the pectoral fins.
A very long free tip trails from the small second dorsal fin.
Young silky sharks often gather near reefs before shifting farther offshore.
They may follow schools of tuna while searching for the same prey.
lookFor: Notice smooth bronze-gray skin, a low first dorsal fin, and long pointed side fins.

name: Loggerhead
tagline: A powerful shell-crusher that crosses whole oceans.
intro: Loggerhead sea turtles are marine reptiles named for their broad heads. Strong jaw muscles let them crush hard-shelled prey that many other ocean animals cannot open.
home: Young loggerheads spend years traveling through the open ocean; older juveniles and adults also forage in coastal bays, estuaries, and continental-shelf waters around the world.
diet: They eat bottom-dwelling invertebrates such as conchs, whelks, crabs, and horseshoe crabs, along with other ocean prey.
size: Adults are about 2.5-3.5 ft (0.8-1.1 m) long and 200-350 lb (90-159 kg) - roughly bathtub-long
superpower: A massive head and crushing jaws turn armored animals into a meal.
funFacts: Loggerheads must surface to breathe air even though they spend nearly all their lives at sea.
Some Pacific loggerheads migrate thousands of miles between nesting and feeding areas.
Scientists estimate that loggerheads may live for 70 years or longer.
Fishing-gear bycatch, marine debris, vessel strikes, and loss of nesting beaches remain serious threats.
lookFor: Look for a large blocky head, reddish-brown shell, and powerful front flippers.

name: Thresher Shark
tagline: Half shark, half tail, and all expert hunter.
intro: SeaPals' thresher shark is represented by the common thresher, whose upper tail lobe can equal the rest of its body. It circles schooling fish and cracks the tail like a whip to stun several meals at once.
home: Common threshers range through coastal and open temperate and tropical oceans worldwide.
diet: They hunt anchovies, sardines, herring, mackerel, squid, and other schooling prey.
size: Up to about 20 ft (6 m), with roughly half being tail—bus length
superpower: A lightning-fast tail slap can stun multiple schooling fishes in one strike.
funFacts: The enormous upper tail lobe is nearly as long as the shark's body.
Threshers sometimes leap completely clear of the sea.
Their small teeth suit swallowing stunned fishes rather than cutting huge prey.
Developing pups hatch inside the mother and eat unfertilized eggs before live birth.
lookFor: The impossibly long, scythe-shaped upper tail lobe is unmistakable.

name: Winter Flounder
tagline: A flat seafloor hunter with both eyes facing up.
intro: Winter Flounder hide in bottom sediment with their eyes exposed. Their dark upper surface helps them blend into the seafloor while they search for small prey.
home: Northwest Atlantic estuaries and continental shelf waters, from Canada to North Carolina.
diet: Small bottom animals, including shrimp, clams, and worms.
size: Can grow longer than 2 ft (60 cm)
superpower: Its left eye moves to the right side as it changes from a larva into a juvenile.
funFacts: Newly hatched larvae have an eye on each side.
Adults move into bays and estuaries to spawn in winter and spring.
Their underside is white.
They hunt by sight during daylight.
lookFor: Look for an oval, flattened body with two eyes on its right side.

name: Spotfin Butterflyfish
tagline: A yellow-finned explorer with a spotted dorsal fin.
intro: Spotfin Butterflyfish travel in pairs or small groups over sandy areas near reefs. Their small mouths reach into crevices to pick out food.
home: Shallow western Atlantic reefs from North Carolina to Brazil; young fish also use seagrass beds.
diet: Anemones, tube worms, tunicates, and other small invertebrates.
size: Up to 8 in (20 cm), though most are smaller
superpower: A narrow mouth and bristle-like teeth help it feed in tight spaces.
funFacts: A black stripe crosses its eye.
Dark bands appear on its body at night.
Young fish have an extra dark band near the tail.
Its flattened body is shaped like a thin disc.
lookFor: Find yellow fins, a pale body, and a black spot near the back of the dorsal fin.

name: Longhorn Cowfish
tagline: A box-shaped fish with an unmistakable pair of horns.
intro: Longhorn Cowfish explore warm reefs looking for small animals. Their angular bodies and forward-pointing horns make them easy to recognize.
home: Tropical Indo-Pacific waters, including the Red Sea.
diet: Sponges, worms, mollusks, small crustaceans, and small fish.
size: Up to 20 in (50 cm)
superpower: It can blow water into sand to uncover hidden worms.
funFacts: It belongs to the boxfish family.
Its front horns resemble those of a cow.
It can release a toxin that discourages predators.
It searches the bottom for many different kinds of food.
lookFor: Spot a rigid-looking, boxy body and two long horns above the eyes.

name: Nurse Shark
tagline: A nighttime hunter that rests along the seafloor.
intro: Nurse Sharks spend much of the day resting in caves or crevices. After dark, they explore the bottom for a meal.
home: Warm coastal Atlantic waters, including Caribbean reefs and the Florida Keys.
diet: Bottom-dwelling animals such as crustaceans and mollusks.
size: Adults commonly average about 7.5-8 ft (2.3-2.4 m)
superpower: Its bottom-feeding lifestyle lets it search the seafloor while many reef animals rest.
funFacts: Resting sharks may gather together in groups.
They often return to a favored daytime shelter.
Their color ranges from yellowish tan to dark brown.
They are most active at night.
lookFor: Look along the bottom for a broad-headed brown shark with a long tail.

name: Yellow-Lipped Sea Krait
tagline: A striped sea snake that also needs the shore.
intro: Yellow-Lipped Sea Kraits hunt among coral reefs, then return to land to rest and digest. Their bodies combine adaptations for swimming and crawling.
home: Tropical Indo-Pacific island shores, shallow reefs, and rocky coastal shelters.
diet: Mostly eels found among the reef.
size: Females average about 5 ft (1.5 m); males are usually smaller
superpower: A flattened, paddle-shaped tail helps propel it through the water.
funFacts: It lays its eggs on land.
It returns ashore to shed its skin.
Its body is wrapped in dark bands.
Females tend to hunt larger eels than males.
lookFor: Find a yellow upper lip, dark body bands, and a flattened tail.

name: Box Jellyfish
tagline: A nearly transparent hunter with a box-shaped bell.
intro: This Box Jellyfish hunts in shallow tropical coastal water. Its almost transparent body can be difficult to see against the sea.
home: Northern Australian coastal waters, including areas near mangrove creeks.
diet: Prawns and other small prey.
size: Bell up to 12 in (30 cm) across, with tentacles reaching 10 ft (3 m)
superpower: It can actively swim toward moving prey.
funFacts: Its bell has a box-like shape.
Tentacles hang in four clusters.
A large individual can have as many as 60 tentacles.
Its transparent body helps it blend into the water.
lookFor: Look for a clear, squared bell with tentacles trailing from its corners.
